Riley Sheehan will spend the next two years of his budding pro career with Netcompany Ineos .

The Coloradan racer and his new team confirmed a two-year deal on Thursday, starting next season.

Sheehan is one of USA’s new generation of rising road racers.

Now aged 26, he became the first American to win the prestigious Paris-Tours one-day classic in what was then his trainee season in 2023.

This year, the powerful all-rounder won twice with his current team, NSN Cycling, and was called up to Team USA before Brandon McNulty won the recent road world championships.

“Joining the team is a dream come true,” Sheehan said Thursday. “It’s a team I’ve looked up to since I was young, and to now be part of such a successful and respected organization is incredibly special.

“I believe I still have so much more to achieve in my career, and having the backing of this team is the perfect next step for me,” he said.

“I’m excited to get started, set ambitious goals and give everything I have to help the team win, while continuing to push myself to become the best rider I can be.”

Sheehan came up through stalwart U.S. squads Aevolo and Rally, and spent a year on the NCL runaway league team.

He turned pro in 2024 and has been progressing since.

“Riley is an exciting rider. He’s fast, technically very skilled and has the ability to perform across a range of terrain,” said Netcompany Ineos head of racing Geraint Thomas.

“We see him being a great addition to our classics group, but he’s also a rider who can contribute right across the calendar,” Thomas said Thursday. “He brings plenty of versatility to the team, and we’re looking forward to helping him continue to develop.”

Sheehan is the latest in a flurry of new signings for Netcompany Ineos.

On Wednesday, the British team confirmed contracts with Clément Champoussin, James Shaw, and former Tour de l’Avenir winner Joseph Blackmore.

Spanish junior supertalent Benjamín Noval will also step directly to WorldTour with the team next year.

But it’s not been one-way traffic at Netcompany Ineos.

Marquee rider Filippo Ganna broke his contract this week to join Lidl-Trek.

The young American contingent of A.J. August, Artem Schmidt, and Magnus Sheffield are among a total of nine riders who will leave the team or retire this winter.

Primoz Roglič , Egan Bernal , Richard Carapaz – rewind to before Tadej Pogačar changed everything, and they were the men to beat.

These three grand tour champions now face uncertain or wildly intriguing futures.

Mountains king and GC threat Carapaz is reportedly due to split from EF Education-EasyPost to join the upstart NSN Cycling Team.

Roglič is being as elusive as ever about his future. We still don’t know whether we’ll see the four-time Vuelta a España winner and Slovenian OG race again.

And Bernal? He’s batted away rumors that he’s going to retire, but he sounded far from convinced.

It could be all-change for three superstars who drove the narrative of the pre-Pogačar era.

Sure, they’re not grand tour favorites any longer, but they continue to influence every race they show up to. What they do next will alter the texture of the sport.

Richard Carapaz is reportedly poised to break his ongoing contract with EF Education-EasyPost to join NSN Cycling Team.

If it happens, it would be the biggest signing of the season, by far.

Rumors have been swirling for some time that Carapaz was considering an early exit from the American EF team. NSN, Netcompany Ineos, and Pinarello-Q36.5 were touted as possible new employers.

Wielerflits reported Friday that NSN Cycling Team – the squad that formed last year out of the ashes of Israel-Premier Tech – won the battle for the Ecuadorian star’s contract. The move has not yet been confirmed.

If it happens, it’s definitely not a transfer we had on our bingo card.

Carapaz has a long leash at EF Education-EasyPost. The 33-year-old chases stages or GC as he pleases. He seems to thrive in the American team’s all-attacking, always-the-underdog environment.

His palmarés from 2026 proves that point. Two stage wins and the polka dot jersey at the Tour de France, and fourth at the Vuelta? Carapaz is doing just fine .

However, according to Wielerflits , Jonathan Vaughters’ team is suffering a budget pinch. Carapaz would be gobbling a huge chunk of the team’s payroll.

Carapaz would change the identity of team NSN in 2027 if Wielerflits’ reporting is true.

Having already signed Santiago Buitrago and Lennert Van Eetvelt, amongst others, the peloton would have a dangerous new climbing team.

What’s going on with Primož Roglič? Nobody knows, and he’s hardly dropping any clues either.

The Slovenian star raced for the last time with Red Bull Bora-Hansgrohe last weekend at Il Lombardia, and has nothing confirmed for 2027.

But old dog Rog clearly has more to give.

Victory at the European time trial championships, a swashbuckling ride at the road world championships, and second overall at the Vuelta a España put an exclamation point on the 36-year-old’s season.

After initial reports that Rogla would race on with the Belgian Lotto-Intermarché team in 2027, Tudor Pro Cycling and Pinarello-Q36.5 are now reportedly also in the hunt for his signature.

Speaking at Il Lombardia last Saturday, Roglič was characteristically cryptic about his future.

“You never know when it is the last [race],” he said.

When asked if he will continue to race next year, he said, “I don’t know yet. We will see. We will see.”

Tudor Pro Cycling and Pinarello-Q36.5 have both been busy on the transfer market this season. Roglič would be a prize addition for either of these rival ProTeams.

Pinarello-Q36.5 in particular has been making waves in this “silly season.” The squad is plundering billionaire backer Ivan Glasenberg’s deep pockets to build a superteam around Tom Pidcock.

Giulio Ciccone and Mauro Schmid headline 11 new signings for the 2027 season. If Roglič is poised to be number 12, he’s not dropping any clues about it.

Egan Bernal to retire aged 29? It was a rumor that rocked the cycling world last week.

According to reporting by contract sleuth Daniel Benson , the former Tour de France and Giro d’Italia winner was contemplating hanging up his wheels for good.

Bernal took only some of the heat out of the speculation last week when he responded with a lengthy Instagram message. The tone was far from conclusive.

“I have a contract with the team through 2029, and for now, my intention is to start next season,” Bernal wrote on Instagram.

Bernal hasn’t raced since the Tour de France. He wrote that after a busy early-season, he had needed time off the grid in summer to reflect on his future.

His statement leaves questions over how long “Bernalito” may remain a pro bike racer.

“I decided to end my season after the Tour de France this year. I needed some time for myself – to rest, relax a little, and regain the peace that can sometimes be lost amidst the pace of racing,” Bernal wrote.

“I want to give myself the time and space needed to face what lies ahead with the same conviction and dedication I have always had,” he continued. “I don’t know exactly what the coming years hold, and I don’t think I need to know everything right now. For now, I want to enjoy the present, experience this moment calmly, and let time take its course.”

Bernal seems at a crossroads in his career, right when it was regaining momentum.

The Colombian star was set back by more than a year after he suffered a terrifying, life-threatening crash into the back of a bus in winter 2022.

Finishing seventh at the Giro d’Italia and winning a stage at the Vuelta a España last summer suggested maybe, say it quietly, “ Bernal’s bac k.” Fifth at Liège-Bastogne-Liège and 10th at this year’s Giro d’Italia reinforced murmurs of a return to form.

Bernal has three more years on his contract with Netcompany Ineos. How many of those he completes seems very uncertain right now.

Paul Seixas is seen as a likely successor to Tadej Pogačar. (Photo: Maarten Straetemans / Belga / AFP) (Photo: MAARTEN STRAETEMANS)

Paul Seixas has made remarkable progress this season, notching up eight wins in all, including a Tadej Pogačar -type dominance of Il Lombardia last weekend.

However although Seixas’ Cannibalesque ascent of the Civiglio saw him break the record Pogačar set four years ago on the same climb, and despite a stunning rate of improvement this season, experienced cycling analyst Sean Kelly feels the world number one shouldn’t lose sleep anytime soon.

Kelly spoke to Velo this week about the two riders and explained why he is believes Pogačar will have the edge for some time yet.

“If you had Pogačar there on Saturday, Seixas probably would have been able to stay with him once again,” he said, speaking of the hilly finale of Il Lombardia. “But then in the flat sprint he doesn’t have any chance, because Pogačar is very fast in a two-up sprint or a little group sprint.

“It’s the other quality that he’s got. As I said many times, Pogačar can do fecking everything.”

Seixas turned heads in Liège-Bastogne-Liège when the then 19-year-old was the only rider able to hold onto Pogačar when the UAE Emirates-XRG rider went all out on La Redoute.

He stayed with him to the summit and then began trading pulls with him afterward. The duo continued together out front until the defending champion put in a last-gasp surge on the climb of La Roche aux Faucons. That finally broke Seixas, but Pogačar admitted afterward that he had believed they’d reach the finish line together.

It’s incredibly rare for any rider to be able to cling on when Pogačar is going all out on a tough climb. It was an even more remarkable achievement for a 19-year-old second-year professional, and it highlighted the extraordinary talent the Frenchman has.

But Kelly insists that even if Seixas is able to remain with Pogačar, that’s only one part of the game.

“There’s no weakness with him where you can say, ‘oh yeah, we can get him on that one.’ They’re just not there. So I don’t think Pogačar is going to be worried.”

There will be some who will disagree with Kelly’s point. They will point to the large age gap between the two riders, a full eight years. They will note that Pogačar has just turned 28, an age when riders are in their prime, and note that it’s very often the time where performances start to plateau and then, a year or two later, start to decline.

Still, Kelly doesn’t think that will be an issue anytime soon. He argues Pogačar will remain the best rider in the sport as long as one thing is in place: motivation.

“Pogačar at 28, 29 or 30 – if mentally he’s hungry enough to do it, I don’t think there’s going to be a problem age-wise,” the former world number one said. “Pogačar definitely has another three or four top years left in him. But will he do four years? Will he have that focus, the mentality to continue on?

“We hear about these long term contracts and that, but in three years’ time, if Pogačar said after the Tour de France, ‘I’m finished, that’s it, I’m stopping at the end of this year,’ it wouldn’t surprise me.”

Pogačar’s ability to stay at the top level is one vital element in any speculation about their future tussles.

The other relates to the Frenchman himself. Kelly acknowledged that Seixas is forging new ground, being the youngest-ever winner of Il Lombardia, and also becoming the youngest rider to start the Tour de France in 89 years.

Those kinds of performances, plus Seixas’ stunning rate of improvement this year—remember, he had no pro wins at all prior to 2025, and now he has eight—lead many to assume that he will leap up another level in 2027.

Hold on, says Kelly. It’s not necessarily accurate to make such presumptions.

“It depends now where Seixas goes from here,” he explained. “Will he continue on improving? Is there much more improvement left in him? Or is he a very early developer, and the level he’s at now is pretty much the level he’s going to be at?

“Maybe that is going to be his best level.”

It seems unlikely that a talented young rider could stop improving, but Kelly believes an error was made this year. He explains what that was and how he thinks it might affect cycling’s most exciting young rider.

“I would be concerned that it was too young to do a Tour de France this year,” he said. “And also to ride it as he did, going for the general classification, every day being there in the battle. His potential might suffer because of doing the Tour de France too young.

“I would be concerned that a guy at 19, doing a Tour of France [as intensely] as they do it now, it could affect his performance next year, the year after. He mightn’t get that potential that would be there if he had been taken along at an easier level.”

Kelly mentions Laurent Fignon as a rider from his era who was incredibly good very young. The Frenchman won the Tour at 22 and 23 but, despite those incredible early performances, never won the race again. He missed out by eight seconds to Greg LeMond in 1989 and won the Giro that same year, but it’s fair to say that his early momentum didn’t lead to the dominance many had predicted.

To be clear, Kelly is wowed by Seixas. He does suggest that slightly sub-par performances by Isaac del Toro and Remco Evenepoel in Il Lombardia made the Frenchman look even better than he was but, nevertheless, he applauds his performance.

He also gives credit where credit is due for the year as a whole.

“You couldn’t but be impressed about the performances. We were hearing about the power outputs that he was doing in training,” he said. “We were hearing all that and then he comes to Pays Basques, the way he dominated there.

“The way he dominated the beginning of the year, that confirmed what we were hearing, what the French were talking him up about. And he’s confirmed all that through the year.…

Christian Prudhomme, far left, pushed back against the idea of shortening the Tour de France. (Photo: Gruber Images)

Shrinking the Tour de France and the other grand tours to make room for the UCI ‘s controversial cycling overhaul?

No way, says Tour boss Christian Prudhomme.

“The Tour de France lasts three weeks, four weekends, and that’s perfectly fine,” Prudhomme told RMC Sport .

Prudhomme said he’s not interested in trimming cycling’s biggest race as proposals to shorten grand tours have kick-started a larger debate over the sport’s crowded calendar.

Speaking just days ahead of the unveiling of the 2027 Tour route, the Tour director defended its current format.

“That question concerns certain grand tours,” he said.

If the Tour vetoes any attempt to tweak the three-week format that dates back to its founding, that leaves the Giro d’Italia and Vuelta a España squarely on the chopping block.

But the bosses of cycling’s other grand tours aren’t buying into the idea to lose a weekend, either.

The debate comes as the UCI maps out potential reforms to professional cycling that could be rolled out by as soon as 2029.

Its “ Agenda 2030 ” consultation drew 55 submissions from teams, riders, organizers, federations, sponsors, manufacturers, and broadcasters.

Unveiled during the Montréal road worlds, the outline covers a broad range of issues that are on the table, including the calendar, cycling’s economic model, fan engagement, rider safety , and the integrity of results via doping controls .

Other ideas include a budget cap, sharing some commercial revenues, and improving broadcasting and marketing to reach today’s social-media savvy audience.

The UCI has since appointed Deloitte as a strategic adviser and the initial reform proposals are due to be presented in December, with the first measures potentially arriving in 2029.

One ideal outcome for backers of shorter grand tours is that the biggest stars like Tadej Pogačar, Jonas Vingegaard, and Remco Evenepoel might race all three rather than just obsessing on the Tour.

Right now, everything is on the table, and no firm proposals have been made.

But one of the most contentious ideas is to squeeze the grand tours into three weekends instead of four.

Some are floating the idea of shortening the Giro and Vuelta to 16 or 17 days, but keeping the Tour at 21 stages.

That idea is not without its supporters.

Some see the Giro and Vuelta dragging on too long sometimes, and the argument is that those extra days could free up some space on the calendar and help some races like Paris-Nice and Tirreno-Adriatico from overlapping.

The other grand tour bosses are having none of it.

New Giro director Luca Guercilena pushed back during an interview with Domestique at Il Lombardia.

“Grand tours must remain grand tours and the Giro d’Italia isn’t going to change. All three grand tours must be the same length,” the Italian said. “There can be no differences.”

The three-week grand tour format is one that grew organically over time. The first Tour in 1903 stretched across 19 days with just six monster stages averaging more than 400km, separated by rest days.

The Giro and later the Vuelta followed, and the grand tours settled into the now-familiar 21-stage, three-week rhythm.

For Guercilena, the brutal third week is the essential ingredient to what decides a grand tour winner.

“Cycling is an endurance sport, and it’s over three weeks that you can truly see if athletes are endurance riders,” he told RMC Sport . “We have no intention of changing that. I understand the UCI and its president, David Lappartient, who believe that overlapping races aren’t good for anyone. But the grand tours must remain three weeks long.”

Vuelta director Javier Guillén drew an equally firm line in a recent interview with MARCA .

“We are not in favor of eliminating any days, not even one. It’s true that the debate is ongoing, but at this time, it is not being discussed at any official or institutional level,” Guillén said.

The Giro and Vuelta have long defended their place alongside the Tour, and resisted any efforts to reduce the number of race days.

Of course, race organizers have a vested interest because every race day comes with lucrative host city start and finish fees, TV rights revenue, and fees from the publicity caravan.

“We believe that the days honoring the great icons of cycling should remain untouched, because otherwise we would all be worse off,” Guillén told the Spanish daily. “There’s no point in doing that.”

The Vuelta moved from April to September and now August in 1995, and the new place on the calendar has helped the Spanish grand tour grow in stature.

For 2027, however, the Vuelta will be contested after the UCI Road World Championships for the first time since the switch to make room for the second edition of “super worlds.”

Seff Van Kerckhove won bronze in the world time trial race in Rwanda in 2025. (Photo: Dario Belingheri/Getty Images)

Visma-Lease a Bike is already building for the post- Jonas Vingegaard era and penned one of Belgium’s most hyped young talents to a long-term deal through 2030.

Seff Van Kerckhove , 18, will join the Dutch superteam’s development squad next season, with a possible fast track to the WorldTour in the works.

Hyped as a potential grand tour talent, the 18-year-old is seen by some as the Belgian prince to Remco Evenepoel . He won 11 races across 2026, including time trials and mountain stages on the European junior racing circuit.

Visma’s development boss sounds keen to give him some breathing room as the Dutch team looks to the future .

“He has shown a strong commitment to his development, and we believe he has the mindset and qualities needed to continue progressing,” said Visma head of development Robbert de Groot. “We believe Seff has the qualities to take significant steps forward over the long term.”

Van Kerckhove missed last month’s worlds in Montréal after a driver struck him during training . Visma said he is recovering well.

He will join newly crowned U23 world champion Ashlin Barry on a development squad that is hardly short of ambition.

The move also takes him out of Decathlon’s orbit. Van Kerckhove raced for its U19 squad, but will head to Visma rather than continue along the French team’s pathway toward a possible future alongside Paul Seixas .

There is a family connection waiting for him, too. Older brother Matisse Van Kerckhove, 20, will graduate to Visma’s WorldTour roster in 2027.

“It is a great honor to join one of the biggest teams in cycling,” Van Kerckhove said. “I believe in the team’s sporting project and am convinced that it offers the ideal environment for me to continue developing and get the best out of myself.”

The signing is another move in the increasingly high-stakes scramble among the WorldTour superteams to secure cycling’s next generation before someone else does.

Riders like Evenepoel, Seixas, and Isaac del Toro have proven that young riders barely out their teens can produce huge results in the WorldTour.

Every team is scrambling to find that next diamond-in-the-rough.

Netcompany-Ineos landed Spanish junior prodigy Benjamín Noval , 18, to join its WorldTour roster in 2027. The son of the former pro of the same name dominated junior stage races, and won double gold at the Montréal junior worlds .

Netcompany-Ineos also signed Patrik Pezzo Rosola — son of Olympic mountain champion Paola Pezzo — to its junior squad for 2027.

Lorenzo Finn , 19, heads to Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe’s WorldTour team in 2027 after winning the Baby Giro and Tour de l’Avenir in 2026.

Another Spanish gem in Héctor Álvarez Martínez, also 19, steps up at Lidl-Trek after two seasons on its development team, a European title, and second place at the U23 worlds.

Most of the major WorldTour teams already fund their own U23 and junior development squads. Otherwise they risk being left behind.

UAE Team Emirates Gen Z will promote Davide Stella — who suffered a brutal high-speed crash at the AlUla Tour — to the WorldTour squad in 2027.

Visma has spent the past half decade building out its development operation that’s already delivering riders who can win straight away.

Per Strand Hagenes is the latest payoff. The Norwegian joined the development squad in 2022, moved to the WorldTour in 2024, and broke through in 2026 with two victories, including Sunday’s Paris-Tours, and second at E3 Saxo Classic.

Matthew Brennan is another Visma development product who enjoyed a blowout 2026. In his second full WorldTour season, the Briton won 12 races, including Kuurne-Brussels-Kuurne and five stages at the Vuelta a España .

Finding the next Vingegaard won’t be easy. Tour de France-caliber riders are the rarest of talents .

The Dane remains under contract through 2028 and turns 30 in December. With two Tour de France titles and victories at the Giro and Vuelta, he’s been at the center of Visma’s grand tour success this entire decade.

There have been unsubstantiated rumors that Vingegaard might want to end his career at Uno-X, the Danish-Norwegian outfit that recently signed Magnus Sheffield as its first American rider .

Van Kerckhove’s signing shows that Visma is clearly thinking about what comes next, even if the team’s sponsorship future remains unconfirmed and after some high-profile backroom reshuffles .

Visma still packs 2023 Vuelta winner Sepp Kuss, Matteo Jorgenson , and rising Italian Davide Piganzoli to carry its ambitions alongside Vingegaard .

Piganzoli, 24, won five races in 2026, finished eighth leading at the Giro, and hit 14th in his Tour debut.

Visma is already moving its chess pieces to stay at the top of the game.

Team Picnic-PostNL has promised to launch an independent investigation into shocking revelations unearthed by broadcaster NOS and the podcast In De Waaier.

The joint investigation by the two Dutch outlets exposed an atmosphere of fear, excessive control, and distrust that dates back more than a decade.

The project involved confidential interviews with 71 current and former Picnic-PostNL cycling team employees, and went live this week.

According to NOS , “many have terminated their employment traumatized. They speak of a ‘culture of fear’ and an ‘unsafe work situation.'”

The partnering men’s and women’s teams have seen superstar riders like Tom Dumoulin, Lorena Wiebes, and Romain Bardet on their books.

The embattled Picnic-PostNL team – which is currently dead last in both the men’s and women’s WorldTour rankings – rushed out a response Thursday.

The team said its offers to cooperate with the investigation by NOS and In De Waaier were ignored, and it promised “to commission an independent, professional investigation” into the allegations.

“In a performance-driven environment such as professional sport, things can go wrong. That is why there are several ways for people within our team to raise problems and concerns. Riders have a personal coach, there is a Rider Committee, and staff members can turn to confidential advisers. If people have felt unsafe within our organization or have felt they lacked sufficient opportunity to raise concerns, we want to understand how that could have happened.

“We are proud of what we have built since 2008 together with the many people who are, or have been, part of and associated with this team. Precisely for that reason, we believe it is important to take a critical look at ourselves.

“We will therefore commission an independent, professional investigation into our team culture. We will take its findings seriously and implement any improvements that may improvements, out of respect for everyone who is, or has been, part of Team Picnic PostNL.”

Picnic-PostNL, formerly known as Team Giant, Sunweb, and DSM, has been stalked by rumors of a controlling, authoritarian culture for years.

Riders have broken contracts amid reports of burnout. Tales have emerged of riders being punished for adjusting their saddle height without authorization, and being forbidden from eating a kiwi.

One anonymous athlete once branded life at the team as a “Soviet regime.”

The long-read investigation published by NOS on Thursday is the most damning indictment of the team yet.

It detailed management taking constructive feedback as an attack on the team’s philosophy. Interviewees described a demeaning attitude toward riders and an unwillingness to flex plans to meet personal needs.

“It became a dictatorship,” said former coach Adriaan Helmantel, who worked with Giro d’Italia winner Dumoulin, amongst others.

In its statement Thursday, Picnic-PostNL outlined its values of safety, collaboration, and fairness, and rejected the claims made in NOS and In De Waaier .

“We do not recognize ourselves in the overall picture presented in the publications,” reads the note.

“The fact that experiences differ does not diminish the seriousness of the accounts that have now come to light. We will therefore commission an independent investigation into how our team culture is experienced in practice and to what extent it reflects the culture we strive for.”

Toss the compression socks, empty the ice bath, and cancel the recovery ride.

A new study has reinforced the theory that the best way to recover from a hard workout might be …. doing nothing.

No freezing cold-plunge. No $100 cryotherapy session. And definitely no compression socks.

A new study on endurance athletes suggests that sitting on the couch, eating well, and sleeping plenty might be just as effective as any costly, time-consuming recovery modality.

The researchers’ findings should have you rethink how you plan to recover from your next heinous interval session or gravel fondo.

Because while the study doesn’t definitively disprove certain recovery tools, it significantly questions the confidence of the claims used to sell them.

Investing time and money in compression socks, ice baths, cryotherapy sessions, and electrostim devices might be buying you little more than belief.

The premise that “you don’t overtrain, you under-recover” has driven an obsession with recovery hacks among cash-rich, time-poor amateurs who’re chasing easy gains.

Someone’s always selling a new “best way” to dodge DOMS, feel eternally fresh, and hit personal bests, every day.

What’s in the body, what’s in the mind? Was it the 10 hours of sleep or the four-minute cryotherapy session that saw you right after your most recent 100-mile ride?

Beyond that, the science behind many popular recovery tools rests on weak conclusions or is muddled by conflicts of interest.

A new independent paper published in August tries to cut through the noise.

By focusing on well-trained athletes who typically recover better than desk jockeys, it narrows the therapeutic window and reduces the chance for confounders. And unlike any previous review, it reports the certainty of its findings.

Take a breath before you read it: “ Physical recovery modalities in competitive and elite endurance athletes: a systematic review and network meta-analysis finding limited evidence of benefit over passive recovery .”

The study pooled trials of 273 “competitive, elite, or professional” cyclists, runners, swimmers, triathletes, and cross-country skiers. The mixed-sex cohort spanned a range of ages.

And don’t think the findings might not apply to you, dear reader. The minimum VO2 Max score required for inclusion was more than achievable for most athletes who “train” rather than tootle. These weren’t all Tour de France pros and Ironman champions.

Subjects were rated for DOMS (delayed onset muscle soreness), creatine kinase (a marker of muscle damage), performance restoration, and a number of other recovery markers after they used one or many popular recovery tools.

All the hip recovery modalities, and some old-school favorites, were put to the test.

The study focused on cold-water immersion, cryotherapy, neuromuscular electrical stimulation, massage, compression garments, and active recovery (i.e., an easy ride).

The comparators? Passive recovery (i.e., doing nothing) and, as a sham intervention, immersion in a room-temperature bath.

The experiment’s conclusion is bad news for your trusty compression socks. It doesn’t do much for the burgeoning recovery technology industry, either.

The headline? No recovery tool can claim to be better than doing nothing.

“In competitive and elite endurance athletes, no physical recovery modality has been shown to outperform passive recovery on any outcome we examined,” reads the summary.

“For sport-specific performance, the evidence goes further: compression garments, active recovery, and neuromuscular electrical stimulation can be said, with low to moderate certainty, not to produce a clinically important benefit.”

The study also failed to find any comparative benefit of one recovery method over another. A $100 cryotherapy session might be no better than a 30-minute recovery ride.

But that said, this isn’t the brink of armageddon for ice baths, compression socks, or Ridley Scott-inspired cryotherapy chambers.

The study’s findings are far from conclusive, despite using 47 comparison trials across nearly 300 athletes.

The authors themselves point out several weaknesses in the methodology and complicating factors in the interpretation of the results. Indeed, result certainty was rated “very low” in 31 of the 47 trials comparing a recovery tool vs. doing nothing.

The one “moderate-certainty” finding might raise eyebrows, however. It might also reduce the average sock height in the finishing area of your next gran fondo or post-race flight.

The evidence concluded with reasonable certainty that compression garments – the cheapest, easiest, most accessible recovery modality out there – do not improve performance.

Recovery, however, is not all in the legs.

The placebo effect of any recovery modality is strong.

That’s why, in the science-backed Tour de France, you still see riders shivering in ice baths after a stage and staggering around hotels squeezed into compression socks.

As Tudor Pro Cycling trainer James Spragg once told Velo :

“Some of the things riders use in recovery could also be considered placebos, or aren’t so well-proven. But to be honest, we don’t care if some things in the recovery protocol ‘work’ or not, just as long as riders feel it’s a benefit,” Spragg said.

“If a rider feels more confident for the next day as a result of something in their recovery process, it’s all a benefit,” he added.

As Spragg said, belief is a powerful component of recovery, as it is of performance.

Many studies have found that recovery methods with the most noticeable sensory effect typically have the strongest influence on reported outcomes.

For example, the pressure of a compression sock or the shock of an ice bath might convince athletes they’re primed for PRs in their next workout.

The new paper reinforces the placebo theory by using a room temperature bath as a “sham” intervention.…

A year ago, a longtime US senator was not thinking much about data centres. ​​

Now, according to one of his advisers, he is having regular meetings with staff to track their impact and working on new legislation aimed at curbing their rapid expansion across the country.

"This happens sometimes, something starts slow and then it goes fast", the senior policy adviser to the Democratic senator told the BBC. The person spoke on condition of anonymity as they are not permitted to speak to the press.

The 180-degree turn in this senator's attention was driven almost entirely by a growing wave of public backlash that has seen politicians across the country scramble to keep up. Public sentiment has turned against the expansion of data centres, the large warehouses that store processing power needed for internet activity.

Packed with rows and rows of computer chips, sometimes seven-feet high, data centres have turned into more than infrastructure for the internet. They are now the physical embodiment of the recent and explosive growth of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, and the varied fears people associate with it.

"I don't want to be the guinea pig for this," Indiana resident Angelita Soriano told the BBC.

A backlash over data centres is another threat to the AI juggernaut

A new Amazon data centre is being built directly across the street from her home. When complete, the 26-building structure will take up more than a square mile in her neighbourhood and maintain 782 diesel-powered generators.

Some data centres are even larger. In Ohio, a joint effort between OpenAI, Nvidia, SB Energy and the US Department of Energy is set to build a data centre complex that will stretch for roughly six square miles, the same size as most townships in the US.

There are about 3,000 data centres currently operating in the US, with that number potentially doubling in the next few years, according to a report by , external Pew Research Center.

Data centres are built through very local rules and permits, meaning federal lawmakers like US senators have little say in the process.

Yet, opposition has become so strong so quickly in the US that suddenly, politicians at all levels are now all but required to take a stand.

"This isn't just an issue on the left, there is huge pushback among conservatives to data centres," Chloe Autio, an AI policy adviser, said. "Whoever articulates a clear position and sticks to it, in either party, really stands to benefit."

Her analysis was echoed by the adviser to the US Senator working on data centre legislation.

"There is a clear policy need here that we're looking to fill," he said. "This is a major backlash across the country - constituents are seeing the impacts of data centres and they do not like them."

That has put many on Capitol Hill - even Republicans - in direct conflict with President Donald Trump, who has championed the unrestrained growth of AI technology.

Trump has dubbed the backlash to data centres a "sick conspiracy" and said people and towns working to keep the buildings out are "backwards and poor".

His ire has been used as a boon to Democratic politicians looking to draw midterm votes from unhappy or undecided constituents.

The BBC spoke to residents of Indiana, Arizona, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Oregon, all of whom have been organising locally against the development of data centres. They expressed concerns about many aspects of the buildings, including their size, construction and operational noise, their impact on air, water and energy resources, as well as the speed at which they seem to be approved by local authorities.

During the first few months of this year, community groups organising against data centres more than doubled to 833, cropping up in almost every US state, according to research from Data Center Watch. The firm collects data for AI industry stakeholders and is part of an AI startup 10a Labs.

Stephanie Maldonado, the political director of LUCHA, a community organising group based in Arizona, referred to the push back against data centres as "a David and Goliath story" that began several years ago.

"People have been ready to put a stop to it," Maldonado added. "Now, people are angry."

New national polling , external shows that AI regulation and data centres are among some of the top issues for voters this election cycle, behind the ongoing Iran War and various aspects of the economy.

Proponents of building data centres often argue the projects will create more, and better paying, local jobs.

Yet, recent research , external from Brookings Institution, a non-partisan policy research group, found that a new data centre creates between 100 and 200 local jobs, which is "fewer than industry advocates claim". The projects also have essentially no impact on local wages.

Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs was one such proponent - until public pressure pushed her to the other side of the issue. In July, she enacted a three-year pause on any new tax break given to a company for a data centres project.

Arizona is far from the only state to see politicians react to data centre backlash.

Abdul El Sayed, a Democrat running for Senate in Michigan, made new rules and regulations for data centres a clear part of his successful primary campaign for Senate.

In the race for governor of Georgia, a Democrat who is calling for a pause on data centre development is in a dead heat with a Republican who disagrees.

"Il pleut des cordes," say the French when it's raining hard.

"It's raining ropes," is the direct translation. It's the kind of idiom which can trip up an AI translator.

"You can imagine the dilemma this throws AI into," says François Yvon, a research director specialised in automatic translation with the French National Centre for Scientific Research CNRS.

He says a well-trained system will know that ropes are not literally falling from the sky and use the English phrase "it's raining cats and dogs".

"But is it going to find the equivalent when it's translating into Indonesian?" asks Yvon.

A comment on the weather is pretty low-risk, but more and more translation is being done by machines, and on topics with higher stakes than the weather.

In April, Google said people are now translating , external one trillion words a month with Google Translate.

That doesn't count the others: DeepL, Microsoft, Claude, ChatCGT and Gemini, not to mention made-to-measure corporate translation systems.

Direct sales of machine translation , external (i.e. outside general AI subscriptions) were worth an estimated $1.4bn (£1bn) last year.

"For plenty of use cases, raw AI translation is now the right call: multiplying your costs by 100 to catch the last few percent of errors isn't rational if you're translating internal documents or product listings," says John Zimmerman, founder of OKA (Open Knowledge Association), a Swiss non-profit that translates Wikipedia articles into other languages.

"For an encyclopedia it's different. Wikipedia runs on trust. A wrong fact can sit there for years and get cited by journalists and AI systems," he says.

With more than 10,000 published pieces, mostly into Spanish, Portuguese and English, OKA is, Zimmerman says, the single largest contributor of translated articles to the collaborative online encyclopedia.

Which is something it absolutely could not have become without AI.

"Translating 10,000 articles the traditional way would cost millions. In our process, the AI produces the draft, then a human translator checks every sentence," he explains.

But that human input is required less and less.

"The machine output is now good enough that skipping the human entirely has become a serious option, and a real temptation across the industry. Two or three years ago, with tools like DeepL, our translators still rewrote a good chunk of every draft.

"Today the prose often doesn't need fixing at all. So, the question is no longer whether AI translation is good, it clearly is, but whether it's good enough to remove the human," says Zimmerman.

Ariella Baltié is a translator and legal expert specialised in translating court documents from English into French.

She was contacted recently by someone who'd already translated his documents with AI, asking her to check them.

"There were two major errors right at the beginning," she said.

The AI had translated "Le demandeur" (the plaintiff) as "the requester". "Totally awkward for legal papers," says Baltié.

When the AI saw "Madame X, épouse Y" (Ms X, wife of Y'), it came up with "Ms X marries Y".

In other words, it mistook a noun for a verb, completely losing the meaning of the phrase.

The consequences of mistranslation in the legal sphere can be serious. In the US, for example, errors in machine-translated asylum applications have led to delays in the release of detainees.

Accuracy is a matter of life and death in the medical field.

"The units for dosages and blood tests often include Greek letters," says Carol Bereuter, who is a specialist in medical translations.

She came across one automatically-translated text that had translated the greek letter μ as milli (one thousandth) instead of micro (one millionth).

"That's a serious error. If you give someone a milligram when it's meant to be a microgram, you are giving them a thousand times the dose," points out Bereuter.

She also makes the point that, as AI translators have got better, catching errors has got more difficult.

"Whereas in the past, with things like Google Translate, the sentence would jump out at you because there'd be a grammatical error or it would sound clunky, today it sounds perfectly legitimate. It sounds fluid. It sounds natural. So the errors are a lot harder to spot."

"If it's something that will bear your signature, there's a risk for your reputation. And if decisions are going to be taken on the basis of a translation concerning a medical procedure, a contract you might sign or a major purchase you might make, the risk is even greater," warns François Yvon.

Even sentences that seem quite clear to a human can trip up an AI service, he says.

"When you have words with different meanings, it's usually very clear for a human which one applies because they understand the context, but when a machine translator comes across the sentence 'translate into Polish', for example, it is quite capable of deciding it must be all about shoe cream, says Yvon.

Context is often crucial. If an AI translator hasn't grasped that we're talking about a football match it is liable to mis-translate "taking a corner".

Last year OKA ran a study, funded by Wikimedia. It studied 119 articles, 10 language pairs and more than 1,000 hours of translator work.

"27% of the AI-generated text still got corrected before publication. Three quarters of those corrections were errors the AI introduced, and 5 to 6% of errors changed the meaning of the original text," says Zimmerman.

Eradicating those errors is likely to be challenging.

"As things stand, I think the fundamental way these systems function makes it quite hard to imagine how they could become 100% reliable," says François Yvon.

This is because probability is a crucial part of the way AI translates each word rather than another and what is probably correct is not the same as what is correct. Especially in the realm of something as subtle and surprising as language.…

Senior banking executives have told the BBC they expect the sector to be "on the menu" when the chancellor announces his Budget in two weeks' time.

John Healey has described the banks as part of "the crown jewels" of the UK economy, yet has refused to rule out a raid on the sector.

The biggest four banks collectively made around £15bn profit in the first six months of this year, leading to calls from trade unions and others for additional taxes.

However, the banking sector trade body, UK Finance, warned that "further increases in bank taxes would weaken competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government's ambition to deliver growth in every postcode".

What is the Budget and what could be in it?

The UK's biggest banks and building societies currently pay a surcharge of 3% on top of the baseline 25% rate of corporation tax, plus a levy on the assets held on their balance sheets.

The sector contributed nearly £40bn to the Treasury last year, if income tax on employees is factored in.

The bank levy generated £1.4bn last year and the surcharge a further £1.2bn.

There are a number of ways the chancellor could extract more money from the sector.

The 3% surcharge was reduced from 8% under Rishi Sunak when he was chancellor, at the same time as he raised corporation tax from 19% to 25%. Returning the surcharge to its previous level could raise around £2bn a year.

The bank levy currently charges 0.1% on outstanding short-term loans and 0.05% on longer-dated loans, although mortgages are excluded from the calculation.

In the past banks have successfully argued that higher taxes would risk making the UK uncompetitive with other jurisdictions and would reduce their ability to lend, and therefore be anti-growth.

In truth, banks were pleasantly surprised they were not hit at the last Budget, given the large profits they have been making in recent years. Rising interest rates have expanded the margin between the rate at which they lend to customers and the rate they pay savers.

There is another option that has been discussed with Treasury officials. Currently banks can use losses from the past to offset against profits - thereby reducing their tax bill in any given year. Lloyds in particular has been a beneficiary of this policy, as large losses from the financial crisis have been used to lower tax bills ever since.

Some analysts and bank executives have pushed the idea of a moratorium on this practice for a few years, which would yield an estimated extra £1bn per year for the Treasury. That would provide a windfall while being "a lot more bearable", in the words of one bank executive.

It would also spare foreign banks from an additional hit, including JP Morgan, whose chief executive Jamie Dimon has warned that the UK already has one of the highest tax burdens on banks in the world. He warned that adding further sector-specific taxes could discourage investment and damage competitiveness.

However, industry leaders say any form of tax rise that hits UK banks and exempts foreign banks' operations in the UK would be hard to square with the government's push to back British business.

Whatever form it takes, banks believe the chancellor now has much more of an appetite to take a larger slice of their pie.

Jess Bacon does all her clothes shopping online.

As a plus-size woman, she finds the size ranges available in stores unreliable. "The sizing in store is notoriously bad. I find it quite demoralising in store," she says.

"The average size woman in the UK is a size 14 or a size 16. I think a lot of people just don't feel seen or represented," says the 29-year-old from Peterborough.

Jess, a culture journalist and author, finds shopping online "much quicker than going into a store, paying for parking, trying things on".

And she feels posting back items that don't fit is less hassle than returning in store, while frequent visits to her local post office give her "more of a community connection".

Jess notes Primark is one of the few High Street retailers where plus-size people can shop. In her experience, Primark stores usually stock up to a size 22.

But soon she'll have the option of staying home even for this - as, after years of holding out, Primark now plans to launch a home delivery service in Britain .

Even throughout the Covid-19 pandemic, when shops were closed, Primark didn't offer the ability to shop online. In 2022 it launched a click-and-collect service, but shoppers still had to travel for their purchases.

The retailer has not said when it expects to launch the service, but has bought a warehouse in Sheffield to enable it to ship products to homes.

Analysts say the decision shows Primark is facing major challenges from ultra-fast-fashion brands such as Shein.

Online shopping had been on the rise even before the surge seen during the pandemic.

Online accounted for 27.3% of all retail sales in August this year, according to the Office for National Statistics, up from 18.1% in August 2019.

Internet shopping has also been boosted by the decline of the High Street in many parts of the country, something which Jess has noticed in Peterborough. "We don't have John Lewis [anymore]. There's kind of not that much of a reason to go into town."

Like Jess, Julia Mitchell, who lives near Chichester, doesn't enjoy in-person clothes shopping. She finds it overstimulating and thinks there are better bargains to be had online.

"I basically never go into them [clothes shops]. It's not really something I enjoy," the 32-year-old says.

"I guess some people might be able to see stuff and pick it up and look at it, but for me, being able to get the best price is more important."

Julia, a content creator, tries to shop ethically and most of her purchases are second hand from Vinted.

The one thing she never shops online for, though, is books. "The thing about bookshops is that they are cultural spaces and community spaces."

Sandra Davies does all her shopping online. She has had three strokes and finds walking to and around stores too much physically.

"I've tried it on two occasions but on both times, standing in a queue for over 10 minutes was too much for me and I collapsed."

The 61-year-old from Sheffield says waiting for deliveries can be taxing as well, as she worries about missing the postie and having to reschedule.

Julie Palmer, a retail analyst, is not surprised that Primark has finally moved into home deliveries as it has evidently recognised that "online sales bring scale".

However, she says a shop's returns policy for online purchases can "make or break" it. Many brands offer hassle-free returns, which Palmer says Primark must match in order to compete.

"Shoppers want them to be free, simple and quick. That means a generous window, lots of drop-off options and refunds that land within days, not weeks.

"When a policy is clunky or slow, customers remember it and shop elsewhere next time."

But returns are expensive for retailers. Some, like Asos, have started charging a fee if customers make frequent returns.

This is a balancing act, Palmer says, "because a fee can easily push a customer to a competitor".

"Most retailers that charge still offer free returns in store, which is a deliberate way to get people through the door and hopefully spending again."

On the underside of most children's toys on sale in the US you'll find the same three words – "Made in China".

Nearly eight in 10 toys (78.3%) imported into the country in 2024 came from China, according to US government figures. , external

Last year, toys imported from China were worth $9.8bn (£7.4bn), trade figures show. , external

With Christmas on the horizon, the toy industry in the US and elsewhere is about to have its busiest time of the year by far.

As retailers prepare their stocks for the festive rush, be they online giants or "mom-and-pop" physical stores, the BBC World Service's Follow the Money series traces how a toy gets from a factory in China to the US. And where the money goes.

Guangdong province, which neighbours Hong Kong in southern China, is the heart of the country's toy manufacturing industry.

In the city of Dongguan workers on the floor of the Mihox factory pop plastic toys out of steel moulds, and pile them into crates ready for painting.

The company says it employs more than 800 people and makes around 55 million toys a year for the American market, which represents half of its business.

Follow the money: The journey of a $30 toy from China to America

Every toy starts with a design from a customer, such as an American toy company. The factory then makes a prototype, and builds moulds from which plastic parts and other components are formed.

Going from the first idea to finished toy takes one to two years, says Melanie Wang from the Mihox sales team. Much of that is the customer going back to the drawing board. "They modified the design again, again, and again to improve it."

Once the design is signed off, things move more quickly. A mould takes about a month to make, and the production run lasts about three months.

So, how much of the US retail price does the factory get? "About 20%," says Wang.

On a $30 toy, that's $6, which has to cover the price of the plastic and other materials, production costs including wages, and what profit the factory makes.

Chinese factories typically make a profit of between 3% and 10%, according to Jay Foreman, chief executive of US toy firm Basic Fun. So for a $30 toy that's between 60 and 18 cents of the $6 the factory charges to make it.

Samson Ko is president of the Toys Manufacturers' Association of Hong Kong. Many of his members moved their factories across the border into mainland China in the 1980s, attracted by cheaper land and labour.

He says the way toys are made has barely changed since then. "Automation now takes place mostly in the moulding and the packaging process. But for soft toys, or even some of the electronics nowadays, it's still very labour intensive."

And Chinese labour isn't cheap anymore, he adds, after recent rises.

Average pay in Vietnam is about half of that in China, said one report , external at the start of this year.

Yet fewer than 10% of Ko's members have moved any production outside China, and in those cases mostly only because customers asked them to do so.

The Chinese factories remain busy, he says, because a single toy can undergo more than one manufacturing process, from moulding the parts, to adding electronics, sewing materials, and final assembly. This often requires it travelling to different factories.

Ko adds that in Guangdong these separate facilities are located close to each other, and used to "working in harmony". He says this makes the whole manufacturing process run more smoothly than in other countries.

From the factory, the toy goes by truck to a port, such as Shenzhen, the biggest in Guangdong.

Ivy Tse is co-founder of FreightAmigo, a Hong Kong logistics company that runs an online platform for both Hong Kong and mainland China exporters. These businesses can book a cargo container, sea passage to an overseas destination, arrange insurance cover, and secure finance.

Tse says it takes about 15 days for a cargo ship to get from Shenzhen to the US west coast, and 25 to 30 days to the east coast. This year's Christmas toys left China in August and September.

Freight, from factory to the US, usually adds about 10% to the manufacturing cost of a toy, adds Tse. So if we stick to a toy that retails for $30 in the US, and therefore costs $6 to make in China, the cost of getting it to the states is 60 cents.

Once the toy reaches the US there is currently a tariff on Chinese toys that has to be paid to the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP).

Following talks between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping last month, the two governments have recommended toys for lower tariffs. But no new rate or start date has been set, and the US must first hold a public consultation. For now the basic rate is 12.5%, and some toys pay more.

This is charged on the manufacturing price of the toy, not on how much it retails for. So for a $30 toy, that basic rate is 12.5% of $6, which is 75 cents.

This tariff is paid for by the American company that has imported the toys. One such firm is Learning Resources, a family business based near Chicago that sells educational toys. Half of these it imports from China.

"We pay 100% of the tariffs, let there be no doubt about that," says the company's chief executive Rick Woldenberg.

The cost of making the $30 toy, getting it to the US, and paying the import tariff, comes to $7.35. So that leaves $22.65, or 75.5% of the total.

That money never leaves the US, explains Foreman from Basic Fun. His firm, which is based in Florida, makes Tonka trucks and Care Bears cuddly toys.

"It's kept by my company, the [US] transportation company, the retailer," he says.

If we allow $2.65 for the US delivery firm, the toy company and the retailer will typically share the remaining revenues 50-50. So that would give them $10 each.

While profit margins are commercially sensitive and therefore not generally revealed, industry studies show that the toy firm and retailer would usually make a profit of up to 25% or $2.50.…

A charity that raises funds to provide children with "essential items" has said families are facing "changing pressures" as celebrates its 25th anniversary.

Help a Guernsey Child said since it was created in 2001 it has provided more than £1.2m worth of essential items, equipment, services and support to local children and young people.

The charity said in its early years it gave financial support to a number of larger community projects benefiting children but there was now an increasing focus on helping individual children and families.

Alex Jenner, from Help a Guernsey Child, said: "Over the past 25 years, we have seen significant changes in the types of support families require."

Jenner said despite changes in needs the charity's "purpose has remained the same, to ensure that children in the Bailiwick are not disadvantaged because they lack the essentials that every child deserves".

The charity said it works through professional referrers who know the children and families involved.

Applications for grants come in from social workers, health visitors, teachers, doctors, nurses and other frontline professionals and are considered individually by the charity's Directors.

The charity said the increasing focus on helping in individual cases meant providing something as "fundamental as a bed, flooring, white goods, clothing, safety equipment or a heating appliance, as well as specialist disability equipment and educational opportunities".

It added the nature of their work reflected the "changing pressures" faced by local families.

These included the rising cost of living and increased demand for essential household items and practical support, it said.

Jenner said: "A relatively small grant at exactly the right time can make a profound difference to a child's safety, wellbeing, education or independence."

Would you use AI to help you write a CV or cover letter? How about during an online assessment or video interview for a job?

We are increasingly using the technology to help us with job applications, graduates , external and recruiters say, with many employers happy for us to do so within reason.

But when does it cross a line from being acceptable to unethical, or even cheating?

Tom, 22, from Maidstone graduated last year with a geography degree and says he applied for over 200 jobs before finally landing a role last month as a restaurant manager.

He says the process was "exhausting" and "demoralising", with employers often not even getting back to him, and he wouldn't have got through it without some help from AI.

"Employers want you to put your absolute best into the application, but if I'm applying for 10 to 20 jobs in a day, the reality is you can't do that."

While Tom says he never used the technology in an assessment or interview, he did use it to help him with cover letters and CVs or to find the right "buzz words" that early stage screening in a recruitment process will pick up on.

He also thinks it's "hypocritical" for companies to ask candidates not to use AI when some are using it themselves to screen candidates .

"That's where it feels like a weird tightrope. You can't use AI too much because otherwise you're not human. But if you don't write like an AI, you may get skipped by the AI screening."

This summer, the Institute of Student Employers (ISE) surveyed 155 of the UK's biggest graduate employers and found they were becoming "more accepting" of candidates using AI during recruitment "at some stages of the recruitment process".

According to the trade group, the most commonly accepted use was writing cover letters or CVs, followed by completing online application questions.

However, it also found some 92% of employers had encountered or suspected AI "misconduct" in the job selection process - up from 85% last year. Most commonly this included using AI as a real-time assistant during online video interviews or to complete online assessments.

On top of this, the tech is also helping candidates write multiple applications at the same time - something known in the industry as "spray and pray". And Stephen Isherwood, joint chief executive of the ISE, says it is "driving up the competition and pressure on students" in an already competitive graduate recruitment market.

Hollie Moody, head of early careers recruitment at energy giant EDF, says she doesn't blame graduates for using AI in applications given how "brutal" the jobs market is right now. But she does think it's becoming a problem.

EDF opened its graduate recruitment scheme three weeks ago, but took the decision to close it early after receiving 12,000 applications - a 10% increase on last year.

Moody says AI almost certainly contributed to this, adding that the tech is being used "a lot more freely" in the actual selection process.

"What we don't have is a level playing field, because what you'll find is that some candidates will absolutely use AI throughout the whole process, and other candidates won't."

Like many firms, EDF now issues guidance on the appropriate use of AI in job applications, and is trying to make its recruitment process as "AI-proof" as possible.

It only reads CVs in the later stages of the hiring process and uses skills and behaviour-based online assessments and video interviews to better assess candidates' skills.

But Moody says some applicants still try to bend the rules, particularly in video interviews.

"A lot of the answers [we hear] are the same. Or people might pause whilst they wait for AI to come back to them with an answer. It's almost like people are reading a script."

AI era 'not all doom and gloom' for graduates, say analysts

Young jobseekers 'discouraged' by ghosting and AI

One recently employed trainee accountant, who didn't want us to use his real name, told the BBC he'd applied for 50 graduate jobs and used AI in every application. But he says it was only for researching roles, tidying up his CV and generating mock practise questions for video interviews.

While he says he would never use the tech to cheat on assessments he knows people who would.

"I know people who have applied for 100 jobs and after a while they become desperate. If they see everyone else is using AI, they think how can I compete?"

According to the ISE, the graduate market has stabilised after a sharp fall last year but remains tough. Graduate roles currently attract an average of 141 applications each, it says.

And while only 16% of employers it surveyed are using AI to screen candidates, more than half plan to introduce it due to the large volumes of applications they are receiving.

EDF does not currently use AI screening but Hollie Moody says they may have to in future.

She says the use of AI in job applications is a "moral dilemma" that employers and employees will continue to grapple with. But she stresses it cannot replace what her firm is looking for in new recruits.

"It's about authenticity, but also personality. We want diversity of thought in the business."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c64g.txt:
On 23 August, Cooper Freeman had no idea clouds above his head were being filled with a silver compound in order to cause rainfall.

Neither did thousands of other residents in Homer, Alaska, who later discovered San Francisco start-up Rainmaker conducted an experiment in that region using cloud-seeding technology.

The company claims it produced 19 million US gallons of water in the sky in three hours.

This approach to weather modification, now more than 80-years-old, involves using planes and drones to disperse compounds such as silver iodide into clouds to form ice crystals. Those crystals eventually become large enough to fall as rain or snow, depending on the temperatures below.

Essentially, cloud seeding speeds up the natural process of water vapor condensing inside of clouds. Gravity then pulls those crystals to the ground. The technology, though, needs ideal climate environments, such as mountainous or cold regions such as Alaska.

Freeman, the Alaska director of the Center for Biological Diversity, isn't just concerned Homer residents weren't widely alerted to these experiments. He's sceptical about what was shot into the clouds, and questions how safe it was for both residents and their habitat.

"It doesn't appear that there was any downstream monitoring to verify that this silver iodide didn't impact the environment," he says.

Freeman adds, "Having a company come in to do this seeding isn't going to solve our water woes, and it feels like a distraction from solving the urgent issues related to water conservation."

Concerns are mounting about the challenges surrounding water security. United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said in July "our world is using freshwater faster than it can be replenished , external ", which echoes reports noting how the past five years have led to the driest period for global rivers , external in more than three decades.

Cloud-seeding technology may be a drop in the bucket, as it doesn't create rainstorms. For example, Rainmaker's 19 million gallons equates to around 0.01 inch of rain across 100 square miles.

Nevertheless, more than 50 countries , external are developing programmes to modify the weather and a surge of start-ups are developing systems to create rain.

As well developed and promising as this innovative field has become, these businesses continue to face thorny questions on safety and efficacy, leading to novel approaches with both finding the right material to spray into clouds and how they do it.

Augustus Doricko, the founder and CEO of Rainmaker, is quick to answer any questions on the consequences of how his company uses the silver iodide compound. It's clear he's been asked about chemical safety many times.

He says Rainmaker releases this form of silver at 20 grams per flight, distributed across thousands of square kilometres. "The resultant increase in concentration on the ground is in the parts per quadrillion, way below the threshold laid out by the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] on what is allowable."

Rainmaker's flights use drones to soar into clouds because without clouds, "we can't do anything," he says, pointing to one of the key limits of cloud-seeding processes. Cloud-seeding sessions have to wait for clouds to form to try to coax them into precipitation.

Their drones are outfitted with silver iodide flairs, and when lit the burning atomizes the water particles into a small enough size so they can stay suspended in the freezing cloud for hours, eventually turning into crystals and later rain.

Rainmaker operates in states such as Idaho, Utah, Colorado and areas of the Middle East such as Jordan. Doricko says, "Jordan residents often only have water for hours per week from their utility because of how scarce water is, and it's a privilege to try to help this storied region."

Cloud seeding's roots began in 1946 when researchers from the General Electric Research Laboratory used dry ice as the first seeding agent. A year later, silver iodide was found to be more effective than dry ice, which quickly turns into useless gas.

While seeding agents caused more rainfall, they didn't move the needle much. In fact, sobering statistics point to how patchy this technology can be in what it pours on the ground.

"With the right conditions, cloud seeding squeeze out about an extra five to 10% of precipitation," says Jon Meyer, an assistant state climatologist with the Utah Climate Center.

What was encouraging, though, for the cloud-seeding sector was a landmark 2017 study that found how silver iodide worked as expected, one of the first reports to observe cloud seeding in action using radar and precipitation gauges.

In the past several years, Meyer has been encouraged to see more companies such as Rainmaker bring innovation to an old industry. "Drones [such as Rainmaker's products] present this new avenue," says Meyer, "and they offer a more targeted nature to these clouds we hope will be responsive."

What is sprayed into clouds may also be undergoing a major shift. Recast Systems in San Francisco is experimenting with a type of protein made from amino acids found in the soil, says CEO Olivia Li.

While still undergoing tests at Texas A&M University, this new seeding agent moves Recast away from silver iodide as the go-to compound.

"It's safe, biodegradable and nucleates ice at a higher efficiency than silver iodide," says Li, whose company currently uses silver iodide to seed clouds in several US states.

Meyer is optimistic this technology's trajectory will only continue to rise. "We're going to see more demand for these services as so many regions are experiencing water demand," he says, "and they're going to be looking for ways to help bridge that gap."

A reduced-cost veterinary clinic has treated 160 pets in its first 11 days, according to the RSPCA.

The animal charity's Medway West branch has launched to offer cut-price care for the pets of people on low incomes or receiving benefits.

"Your pet would come first. You'd have a bit of toast yourself and pay out for your pet," said Chatham cat owner Christine Gardner. "Having somewhere like this is amazing."

She told the BBC it was "just really good to have something nearby that I can get to" with her six cats.

Angela Adams said her pets were her "babies", adding: "I would rather starve than they starve."

She said she had eight cats, two rabbits, four guinea pigs, two African land snails and a tortoise, and that she did not know what she would do without the animals, as she was unable to work for health reasons.

"It's very expensive. Seven of my cats were due for vaccine this month and you can imagine the cost of that," she told the BBC. "That's a lot of money."

"I've had friends messaging me struggling, so this place is brilliant for people."

RSPCA branch account manager Imara Ó Niocail said that "a lot of people who were more than capable of affording to have these animals" were no longer able to care for them due to the cost of living or a change in circumstances.

"We would like to keep the animals at home with the owners and treat them there," Ó Niocail told the BBC.

The low cost clinic meant that pet owners in Medway could "seek the treatment that they need and then take the animals home", without having to pay the full vet costs , she added.

Medway West branch manager Kevin Morton said the charity's centres were "full-to-bursting" with animals and some people "give their animals up because they can't afford to look after them".

It's green, bulging and intimidating. Ford's latest vehicle looks like a pick-up truck that has been through an Incredible Hulk transformation. Based on its popular Ranger series, this beefy number parked outside the front door of Ford's Dagenham plant can carry a load of two tonnes, tow up to four tonnes and is also shouldering the hopes of the 2,000-strong workforce that still makes engines here.

Inside the factory, the three-litre diesel engines that will power this camo-painted beast drift down a production line that has seen output cut from 90,000 engines a year to about half that over the last decade.

Ford is hoping that a pivot towards military vehicles can help fill the void created by what the company's UK boss calls the most challenging environment since the invention of the motor car. Once mighty, the European car industry is starting to look puny and is hoping surging defence budgets as Europe re-arms can help it flex its industrial muscles once more.

Ford is part of a joint venture with defence specialists General Dynamics and Ricardo bidding for a Ministry of Defence (MoD) contract to supply 9,000 vehicles over the next five to seven years to replace the Army's ageing Land Rover-based fleet.

Lisa Brankin, chair of Ford UK, says it is a chance to showcase their abilities to respond quickly to defence needs: "As a manufacturer you look at every opportunity that comes at you and this is a great opportunity that we would love to take advantage of."

This is not the first time Ford has busied itself with defence work.

Ahead of World War Two, Ford's factory in Dagenham, east London, was the largest car plant in Europe.

When war broke out, civilian car assembly stopped completely, and the factory was converted entirely to military production. Between 1939 and 1945, the Dagenham plant built 360,000 vehicles for the Allied war effort.

Ford workers in Manchester manufactured 34,000 Rolls-Royce-designed Merlin engines, which powered Spitfires and Hurricane fighter planes.

Eighty years later, the UK and European car industries are hoping that the engines of war can help defend against what one supplier told the BBC was a "terminal decline".

As Europe feels compelled to commit hundreds of billions to ramp up defence spending in the face of the menace from Russia and US reluctance to be Europe's protector, car makers that are under commercial attack from Chinese rivals have taken notice.

So can the rearmament of Europe save an auto industry and a supply chain facing crisis?

Ford is far from the only car company that sees defence as a growth industry - and one that can utilise the growing overcapacity at car plants across Europe.

French car maker Renault has signed a strategic agreement with defence giant Thales to produce military drones - targeting an output of up to 1,000 units per month. The French military and Directorate General for Armament want to tap into Renault's mass-production capabilities to bypass traditional, slower defence supply chains.

Meanwhile, Volkswagen has agreed to sell an under-used factory in Osnabruck, western Germany, which will become a military manufacturing hub in a joint venture with an Israeli-based defence investor.

Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), which makes the Land Rover, is also bidding for the same contract as Ford - as the Army retires its existing Land Rover-based fleet by 2030. JLR has also established a new dedicated business unit to support its global military ambitions.

It makes sense for under-utilised auto manufacturing capacity to switch to defence, says Mike Hawes of the Society for Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) trade association.

The UK car industry and its suppliers are heavily reliant on a few big manufacturers – Nissan in Sunderland, Toyota in Derbyshire, BMW in Oxfordshire and the biggest of them all by value of output, JLR at multiple sites in the Midlands and Merseyside.

And Hawes says the supply chain is very vulnerable.

"UK automotive output has been in decline over the last eight or nine years," he says. "We're probably half of what we were 10 years ago. Now, that's obviously going to hit the supply chain because they're not making the same number of parts. So they've got capacity. They may be quite dependent on one particular manufacturer as well."

So they will welcome "the opportunity to broaden their customer base and potentially move into defence", he says.

Just two weeks ago, JLR announced it was cutting 4,000 jobs from its 30,000-strong UK workforce in order to reduce costs to stay competitive with international – particularly Chinese – rivals. Dave Roberts of the firm Evtec, which supplies cooling systems components to JLR, is worried about the implications of this.

"JLR is the critical mass in the UK automotive manufacturing space," he says. "It is the glue that holds the whole of the sector together. Because remember, when you're making volumes for JLR, they're significantly higher than any other car maker in the UK.

"If they suffer, the ripples run deeper through the supply chain."

Earlier this week, major JLR suppliers urged the government to help automotive manufacturers move into aerospace and defence, warning that large-scale car production in the UK faces long-term decline.

In an open letter to the prime minister, chancellor and West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker, industry leaders argued Britain's automotive supply chain was "not in decline" but "in the wrong market".

The letter was signed by executives representing businesses with more than 8,600 direct employees, alongside the Confederation of British Metalforming, which represents about 75,000 workers.

Signatories to the letter said the redundancies were "the first visible crack" in a UK automotive supply chain supporting about 183,000 manufacturing jobs.…
