Netflix has said it will cut 1,000 jobs globally as the streaming giant faces competition from rivals.

The cuts - the steepest since 2022 - will mainly affect its human resources, legal, product and technology teams and equates to around 6% of its total workforce.

Last month, Netflix 's co-chief executive, Ted Sarandos, told the Bloomberg Screentime summit that the company was "not growing as fast as I want us to".

The streaming industry is going through a period of consolidation following Paramount's $110bn (£83.6bn) merger with Warner Bros, the owner of HBO, while free platforms such as YouTube and TikTok continue to attract viewers.

In an email to staff, Sarandos and co-chief executive Greg Peters said Netflix would "continue to invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation".

Netflix had come close to its own deal with Warner Bros but was outbid in the end by Paramount .

Commenting on the "organisational changes", Sarandos and Peters said: "Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritise our people and resources."

Managers will tell employees whether their job has been cut "soon".

The email added that the firm was on track to meet its financial forecasts. The streaming service is due to report its latest results on 20 October.

Investors have been weighing up user engagement - the amount of time customers spend on Netflix - as it competes with platforms such as YouTube and TikTok.

The firm has been attempting to expand its business, including gaming and allowing adverts to play before and during shows and films.

However, "they haven't been able to find another line of major revenue," said Ross Benes, senior analyst at eMarketer.

He added that the company remains reliant on a subscription business that could be approaching a plateau.

"Eventually, because they're nearing a ceiling with that, they'll need another revenue stream to diversify, and that's where it's been more of a struggle," he said.

The last major redundancy round at Netflix was in 2022, when it cut about 450 jobs after losing subscribers for the first time in more than a decade.

Waiting times for driving tests have dropped below 20 weeks for the first time since November 2024, according to official figures.

But learner drivers in September still had to wait an average of 19.7 weeks, or around five months, for a practical test.

The Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) has been trying to cut waiting times and clear a backlog which began during the Covid pandemic in 2020.

Commenting on the agency's progress, one driving instructor told the BBC: "I don't think this is anything to boast about."

The DVSA initially had hoped to reduce the average waiting time to seven weeks by the end of last year.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander pushed the target back to summer 2026, but subsequently admitted even that would not be possible - with waits not expected to fall to seven weeks until next autumn .

The DVSA conducted 191,682 practical driving tests in September, with more than half of those passing.

Learner drivers have repeatedly told the BBC how a lack of access to driving tests has limited their freedom, education and job prospects.

Until earlier this year, many learner drivers chose to pay inflated prices to access driving tests being resold by third party providers who'd used automated programmes, or bots, to block book tests before learners could access them.

But a number of changes were made to the test booking system earlier this year by the DVSA to stop the system being exploited. Now, only the learner driver is able to book their driving test.

Sophie Stuchfield, a driving instructor in Watford, told the BBC: "Whilst the re-selling of tests does seem to have stopped, which is a massive positive, they've still failed to recruit enough examiners to cope with demand."

She didn't believe that the slight fall in numbers for waiting times "is anything to boast about", adding that in many areas the wait for a driving test when booking is 21 weeks.

"On many occasions, my drivers wake up at 5.45am on a Monday, only to not end up with a test as when they click on something, by the time they put their details in, they are told the test has already been taken."

Sophie added that the waiting time to get a test meant that many learner drivers "who haven't even started driving lessons will book a test knowing it's 5 months away", putting themselves and the instructor under a lot of pressure.

Justin Madders, the minister for roads, said the government "inherited record waiting times and a significant backlog".

"While driving test waiting times are still not where we want them to be, these figures show real progress is being made," he added.

A DVSA spokesperson said the agency was "committed to reducing waiting times" and that "examiner numbers are at their highest level since November 2017".

"But we know there's more to do and we won't stop until every learner can get a test slot when they need one, wherever they're learning to drive," the spokesperson added.

Are you a learner driver waiting for a practical test slot? Tell us your story.

A company has been accused of promising jobs in the healthcare sector which never materialised, leaving people thousands of pounds out of pocket.

Registered in 2025, Synetal Solutions Ltd says it offers career-focused training programmes in the healthcare and IT sectors.

But the BBC has spoken to a number of people who claim they were promised training and support to secure sponsored healthcare jobs that never became available to apply for.

London Citizens Advice says it has seen an increase in recruitment-related scams since the government stopped overseas recruitment for care workers , external . The charity described the firm's practices as "unethical".

Synetal Solutions says it "takes these concerns seriously and disputes the broad allegation that its services or candidate outcomes are fictitious".

Apurv Patel, who has been in the UK on a Skilled Worker visa since 2023, said he paid Synetal Solutions £3,600 across February and March for healthcare training after he and a friend were verbally promised guaranteed sponsored jobs.

Eight months later he has received no job offers, interviews or meaningful employment support, he said.

"I'm frustrated. I paid money, I wasted my time. I did whatever they wanted without any result," he said.

"It's had a miserable effect on my family and finances."

Patel said he did receive some training but described it as poor quality and ultimately "worthless".

Having previously worked for two years as a healthcare assistant, he said he became concerned when a trainer was unable to answer routine questions about care work.

"She didn't give us any answers and we realised she didn't have any experience of healthcare," he said.

The company disputes claims that training was ineffective.

He also alleged communication with the company deteriorated after he made his second payment, with responses sometimes taking several days.

Patel has since complained to his bank and sought help from Citizens Advice.

The BBC has seen emails from the company advertising a "three-month recruitment programme" offering "training and placement with sponsorship" for £5,500.

Home Office guidance , external states agencies may charge for services such as training or CV-writing assistance, but cannot charge fees solely for finding, or attempting to find, employment.

Responding to questions about its marketing, Synetal Solutions said: "We acknowledge the 'guarantee' wording in the emails supplied and recognise that contractual terms alone do not resolve concerns about those assurances."

As part of its programme, Synetal Solutions created accounts for trainees on iHasco, a health and social care training platform.

The BBC contacted iHasco, which confirmed the company was a customer. However, it said its terms did not permit customers to resell its training content to individuals who were not employees.

The company said it was reviewing Synetal Solutions' account and would take appropriate action if necessary.

Synetal Solutions said it had acted in accordance with its agreement with iHasco.

The Care Quality Commission said there was no single qualification that automatically qualified someone to work as a care worker. Instead, providers are responsible for ensuring employees are appropriately trained and competent for their roles.

The BBC also contacted a number of healthcare organisations whose logos appeared on Synetal Solutions' website as examples of employers where graduates had worked.

Those organisations that responded said they had no links to the company. Some also said they had not authorised the use of their branding, and some said they would not accept certificates provided through the company's training.

Daniel Blake, director of London Citizens Advice, described the company's approach as "exploitative".

"The promises that were made are impossible promises," he said. "They are targeting people with vulnerable immigration status.

"This company is asking for large sums of money upfront without any reputable standards, without any reputable evidence of success, and yet when it goes wrong they are refusing to take any responsibility.

"For us, it seems a very unethical way of conducting business."

He added that no reputable recruitment agency would guarantee a successful outcome without first assessing a candidate and matching them to a suitable role, and urged anybody asked to pay large sums upfront to seek independent advice.

"If it seems too good to be true, it probably is," he said.

The company's website states: "Synetal Solutions provides the right support, guidance, and guaranteed job placement to help you succeed."

Its social media channels also promoted healthcare as "one of the most reliable paths" for people seeking visa-sponsored work in the UK.

Sarah and Rahul, whose names we have changed, said they paid £3,000 to Synetal Solutions while seeking sponsored employment before the expiry of their student visas.

Rahul, a former dentist in India, could remain in the UK on a graduate visa for longer, but Sarah's immigration status was close to expiring.

To pay the fee, the couple said they borrowed money from a family friend and took out a loan.

Rahul said he was shocked by the quality of the training.

"The mentor didn't know anything about healthcare," he said.

The couple said they were also shown the names of established healthcare providers, including Bupa, as examples of potential employers. Bupa told the BBC it had no connection with the company.

Synetal Solutions says some of their candidates "told us they had secured employment with Bupa" and the reference was "not intended to suggest a formal partnership with Bupa".

It says it had not verified those outcomes and "cannot attribute the recruitment decisions to our training".

Rahul said he secured one or two interviews, but prospective employers rejected the certificates he had received through the programme.…

There's a weird and wonderful jet flying over the US. It has the nose of anteater, parts cannibalised from other planes and a cockpit so far back the pilot depends on a camera to see where he's going.

This contraption, the X-59, might just be the future of air travel.

The X-59's owes its eccentric design to the problem of sonic booms. The shockwave created by a jet breaking the sound barrier restricted Concorde to flights over the sea and barred it from lucrative routes across the US.

Now Nasa is working around that problem using the X-59's elongated snout to flatten supersonic booms into tolerable bumps in the background.

On top of its bizarre appearance the X-59 boasts a remarkable lineage. It's the latest in a series of experimental Nasa aircraft dating back to 1947 and the first plane to break the sound barrier, the Bell X-1.

Peter Coen, a 43-year Nasa veteran who manages the programme, explains the thinking behind 80 years of X-planes. "Our approach is to pick small goals we aim to prove with flight data and we construct an airframe for that one task."

The X-plane philosophy is to "minimise goals, the more goals you have the more expensive it gets." For the X-59 it's about suppressing sonic booms on a budget and nothing else.

In the case of the X-1, flown through the sound barrier in 1947 by the legendary test pilot Chuck Yeager, Nasa knew a .50 calibre bullet travelled faster than the speed of sound. So the stumpy little aircraft was shaped like a bullet with wings added.

A mere 20 years later the X-15 rocket plane, a cylinder with tiny wings dropped from a B-52 bomber, flew to 6.7 times the speed of sound (4,520 mph) and the edge of space, paving the way for heat-resistant materials vital to the Space Shuttle.

Nasa is flying the X-59 in conjunction with community surveys to assess what people think when a supersonic boom is bent by the planes stretched nose and hushed up.

"We want to figure out what level of boom is acceptable to people on a regular basis," says Coen, who reckons his machine will sound "like a car door being closed across the street" when it flies past Mach 1, around 660mph at airline cruising altitude.

With its cockpit and ejector seat taken from a T-38 training jet, its landing gear from an F-16 fighter and engine courtesy of the F-18 this jigsaw of an aircraft was assembled by Lockheed Martin for Nasa.

A camera feeding a screen in front of the pilot relies on instantaneous computer processing to get round the lack of forward vision. It first flew in 2025 and is now breaking the sound barrier over chosen US towns.

But is there still a place for X-plane projects in a world where relatively cheap drones are being rapidly developed - not least in Ukraine's war against Russia .

Even Nasa considered an uncrewed X-59. But drones are not always a cheaper option.

Removing the pilot would have added the cost and complication of certifying a robot jet to fly fast over urban areas.

Plus the X-59 had to be big enough to resemble an airliner punching through the sound barrier, which in turn allowed space for a cockpit.

Nasa is no stranger to drone X-planes. The X-48, a scaled down model of an airliner that blends wing and fuselage to create a single lifting body, flew in 2007.

Small was beautiful for the tiny X-48 with its 20ft wingspan as this kept the programme within budget.

"It's likely that future X-planes will be uncrewed," says Coen, before adding the vital caveats "unless the technology we're researching relates to piloting or if crewing it is more cost-effective".

Guy Gratton, professor of Aircraft Test and Evaluation at Cranfield University, gets frustrated at the suggestion crewed test planes have had their day.

"There's a belief in certain quarters that drones can do everything. In Ukraine they've done amazing things with drones, but if you want to carry people you can't take short-cuts."

Gratton has tested light aircraft and stresses the importance of a human in the loop. "You lose a huge amount without pilots, you miss lessons a pilot would identify, plus it can take four times as many people on the ground to test a drone."

Staff monitoring signals from a drone are an indirect cost that keeps some piloted X-planes relatively affordable.

The UK has flown its own technology testbeds and Chris Yeo was in the pilot's seat of one. The Experimental Aircraft Programme (EAP) flew from Lancashire in 1986 and tried out core systems for the Typhoon fighter.

Yeo acknowledges the EAP's shared heritage with X-planes. "They all research some facet of flight, and demonstrate the design is working correctly. A lot of people say they can do something, but you only know it works when the design has been tested and certified."

Forty years on from Yeo's EAP flights a new UK technology demonstrator is taking shape. It is, says Tony Godbold who runs the project for BAE Systems, "the X-plane of our generation".

This BAE Systems initiative pulls together 100 UK suppliers including Rolls-Royce to test out ideas that might make it into the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP), a fighter due to fly in the 2030s. The technology demonstrator will borrow engines from the existing Typhoon and fly sometime in 2028.

This has triggered great excitement in the UK's small community of qualified fast jet test pilots. Almost every one, around 14 of them says Godbold, has already tried out this plane on a flight simulator.

For many in the aerospace industry, the human element still matters as much as it did in Yeager's day. "You can model a lot on computers and simulators, but the experience of test pilots is when stuff gets real, we only really learn things when we get their feedback," Godbold admits.

There's a political dimension to such jets too. Godbold says his plane underlines the UK's commitment to GCAP, a joint effort with Italy and Japan. "This proves we are serious in this space."

Some people in the US "still hate the look of solar", Kate Collardson acknowledges.

She would know. Collardson handles operations for the Solar Service of Colorado, a solar maintenance and inspection company. She's also held just about every other job in the industry, from installer to instructor.

For those that hate the look of solar panels, an alternative is a solar roof, where the tiles (or shingles) house solar cells, but look much the same as regular tiles.

This is especially important for historic buildings, where heritage rules limit changes to their appearance.

For many people, the first time they'd heard of this product category was in August, when Tesla's website stopped offering solar roofs , external . This followed disappointing sales and a lawsuit over sudden price hikes , external .

Other companies have also pulled out, but Tesla's decision in particular sent shockwaves through the solar roof industry.

Some see it as a death knell for solar tiles; others, as an opportunity.

For instance, the small Swiss company Freesuns is considering expanding to the US.

Deborah Learoyd, Freesuns' CEO and managing director, estimates that the company's sales have grown 20–30% since it was established in 2019.

In general, solar roof components continue to be manufactured in smaller batches. This limits the economies of scale and standardisation, though flexible manufacturing could help somewhat.

Learoyd says that while the unit costs for Freesuns' products are slowly decreasing, "a lot of the cost is actually the fact that every roof is a little bit different. And so it has to be engineered a little bit differently, installed a little bit differently".

Solar roofs typically require collaboration among roofers, solar installers and electricians. And building regulations tend to be more complex than for solar panels.

The additional time and paperwork can take a toll on a roofing business, Collardson explains. "You try to put a roofer into the equation and they're going, 'This is taking forever. I'm losing money. I could have sold 10 roofing jobs in the time that it takes me to sell this one'."

Collardson has to charge more for repair of solar shingles, compared to a standard photovoltaic (PV) setup.

She explains, "With traditional solar, we generally have electronics on the panel and a map that shows us exactly how much each panel is producing." So when something goes wrong, it's easy to spot where.

"With solar shingles, we don't really have the benefit of that mapping; there's no room underneath the shingle for the electronics." Thermal cameras can identify the trouble spots, however.

But then there's the matter of accessing them. "You can remove the one in the middle of the array, but you have to walk on the others, and you really shouldn't walk on them because you're going to create micro-fractures and that's going to cause issues down the road."

Before repair costs are factored in, a solar roof might cost twice as much as a system of solar panels mounted on a roof.

Solar roofs are also less efficient - one reason is that the tiles are just smaller.

Another factor is the energy lost as heat. Since the tiles sit close to the roof, there's less airflow than with standard solar panels mounted on a roof. Heat impairs solar performance.

Coloured tiles are even less efficient, comments Ben Graves, co-founder of UK solar company Sunsave. "The reason why all solar cells are black, and increasingly the whole panel is now black, is because black is the best absorbing colour."

Overall, much more space would need to be devoted to solar roof tiles to produce the same amount of energy.

Sunsave does not offer solar roofs. "Most people in the UK just don't have enough money to pay for it," Graves believes.

While appearance was a bigger factor five years ago, now "the vast majority of consumers are most interested in how much they can save".

But supporters of solar roofs argue that they should not be pitted against standard solar modules on roofs.

"Let's not compare PV roof tiles to a standard PV system, but look at PV roof tiles as generating additional electricity from our roofs instead of just having the roof sit there," urges Martin Heinrich who leads a research group at the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems in Germany.

While standard solar panels have gone from strength to strength, solar roofs have not advanced to the same extent.

One advancement that could especially help solar roofs is matrix shingling technology.

This is a different way of connecting solar cells. The solar cells are cut into narrow strips, layered like overlapping shingles, and connected to each other using electrically conductive adhesive, rather than metal wires.

This means that the electrical current can flow around shaded areas, unlike with standard modules. "If you get like a bird pooping on a part of the cell, the current can go around it," Learoyd explains.

In addition to increasing energy output, this improves the appearance as the silver wires aren't visible.

Another advantage, Heinrich says, is that "since we cut the cells into smaller areas, we can fill out special sizes more easily. You don't have to adhere to the regular pattern size."

Freesuns is an early adopter of matrix shingling technology in building-integrated PV. "We see it as a big opportunity for the future in terms of how we would make our tiles," Learoyd says.

What would also help the company is better software for automated design. This would speed up the design process, since each roofing job is unique.

Learoyd believes this would lower costs and give "the whole construction industry much more confidence in using the product".

Ten years after her own solar roof was installed, and despite the sector's setbacks, Learoyd remains optimistic.

She believes that for people with the means, it will eventually become standard to install a new roof with some sort of embedded solar. "It's just a no-brainer."…

When the first day of the apple harvest rolled around in Washington State last year, the fruit was ripe and the pickers were ready – but the weather had other ideas.

"It was like 38C… it's not safe for people to work in that heat," recalls Joel Carter at Okanagan Specialty Fruits. "We had to stop at 10 o'clock in the morning."

He says that artificial intelligence (AI) models that forecast ideal harvest dates, taking into account the weather, would be useful. "You need to know more than just when your fruit is going to be ripe. How long do you have to pick it?" he says. "That's where these models are really helpful."

Carter's company has more than 1,250 acres of apple orchards in Washington, and the fruit is grown for sliced apple portions – often sold to hotels and schools, for example. The firm is investing in technology with the hope of maximising productivity. Even the apples are genetically engineered so that they don't brown easily once cut.

But planning a harvest is tricky. New tools that count and analyse fruit on the tree or vine, and predict when crops will ripen, are emerging. It matters because prices for fruit, especially high-value berries such as strawberries or blueberries can fluctuate wildly. Getting the harvest date wrong means you book seasonal workers when you don't actually need them, and risk missing out on the biggest profits.

Okanagan Specialty Fruits is already experimenting with cameras from a Canadian firm called Vivid Machines. The cameras are mounted atop tractors and they scoop up imagery of the apple trees as the tractor trundles by. AI identifies buds, flowers or fruit in that footage.

"Right now, Vivid is telling us crop estimates and harvest dates," says Carter. He notes that the system is good at picking out very tiny flower buds, which are hard to see at a glance with the naked eye.

But the accuracy of forecasts is noticeably dependent on the quality of historical information fed in to the system, adds Carter. "This isn't something where an AI can scrape the internet and figure out what's the average [yield] for Granny Smith," he explains. "It's going to be bespoke to your farm."

Apples are at least somewhat forgiving – the harvest window for those Granny Smiths is three weeks long, says Carter. For other fruit, such as berries, you might only have a few days.

"If a strawberry crop is on, you have to harvest it – otherwise your entire crop gets diseased very, very quickly," says Raymond Martin, co-founder and chief operating officer of FruitCast, a UK company that offers harvest forecasts to fruit growers here.

His firm offers growers crop predictions for strawberries and also raspberries, blackberries, blueberries and tomatoes. "We're moving on to grapes next year," adds Martin.

Don't experienced farmers know when their fruit will be ripe, I ask? Martin says they generally do – but not necessarily across their entire farm, which might be many acres in size, or have both outdoor and indoor growing areas. "We do exactly what the farmers could do but we just do it on a scale that they can't."

The system analyses footage of ripening fruit that can be captured by drones, someone walking up and down a field with a smartphone, or a camera mounted on a farm vehicle.

This year has been challenging, notes Martin, with hot weather and severe drought hitting much of the UK . This has stressed many fruit plants, putting them into thermal dormancy and slowing down fruit production.

The FruitCast model accounts for weather and irrigation conditions in its forecasts. The company says, "our forecasts land within 10% of actual picked volume one week out (90% accurate) and within 17% three weeks out (83% accurate). We guarantee less than 20% error…"

Angus Soft Fruits is one company that has worked with FruitCast. AI tech for forecasting fruit ripeness is not yet "a finished solution" says operations director Neill Finlayson: "This journey is still ongoing and, whilst significant progress has been made, the industry remains some way from achieving a fully integrated forecasting ecosystem."

Driscoll's, a California headquartered fruit seller with a big operation in the UK, also confirmed to BBC News that some of its independent fruit growers in the UK have used FruitCast's technology.

Researchers are also exploring new ways of analysing fruit in intense detail. Many farmers already use handheld brix meters to gauge the sugar content of their crop. These devices work by measuring how much light has changed direction, or refracted, after passing through a liquid – indicating the volume of solids present.

Some such meters use infrared light, meaning there's no need to cut into the fruit to take measurements. But Yasaman Ghasempour at Princeton University says millimetre waves, high frequency radio waves, can penetrate deeper "They basically respond very well to humidity, water [and sugar]," she says.

She and her students have come up with a millimetre wave-based ripeness detector , external that could be used by farmers – or even customers searching for perfectly ripe fruit in shops. Her students tried it out at a local market in New Jersey. "[Staff] there got kind of scared that we were doing something shady," laughs Ghasempour.

Such fine-grained analysis of fruit, if currently unripe, could also help inform forecasts of when it will be ripe.

But while some growers, such as Carter, are interested in trying out new tech, many will wonder whether investing in it is really worthwhile. "Adoption is very complicated," says Jing Zhang at North Carolina State University. "The grower has to have confidence in the research and whether or not it works."

Zhang has been working on a system to automatically count the number of blueberries , external captured in smartphone images of blueberry bushes.…

The UK's economy recorded surprise growth in August despite the impact of rising energy prices and borrowing costs.

Official figures showed the economy expanded by 0.1% in the month, defying analysts' expectations of a slight contraction.

It means the economy grew by 0.7% in the three months to August, and follows an upgrade to this year's forecast for the UK economy from global watchdog the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

Chancellor John Healey, who will deliver his first Budget in two weeks, said the UK has shown resilience in the face of conflicts in Europe and the Middle East.

Britain's economy was boosted in August by an increase in production, which includes manufacturing, oil and gas extraction and energy supply.

The services industry, which makes up the largest chunk of the UK's economy, was flat during the month, while the construction sector contracted.

Over the three months to August, the UK's economy grew by 0.7% overall. ONS director of economic statistics Liz McKeown said computer programming had been the biggest contributor to what she described as "robust" growth over the period.

But she said the production and construction sectors shrank over the three-month period.

August's surprise expansion follows growth of 0.4% in July. The ONS also upgraded its estimate for June's monthly growth to 0.4% from 0.3%.

Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said Britain's economy was "more robust than we thought".

He warned that an expected increase in inflation would still "dampen growth", but added that the economy was showing "remarkable resilience to higher energy prices and borrowing costs".

PwC senior economist Jake Finney said the development of AI infrastructure was underpinning Britain's relatively strong performance.

"The UK still lags the US in both the scale of that investment and the boost it provides to growth, but it is making progress and remains ahead of many of its European peers," he added.

The latest growth figures were released after Healey landed in Bangkok for the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

Earlier this week, the global financial watchdog praised the UK's plans to cut debt levels, with global borrowing costs on the rise, with managing director Kristalina Georgieva adding that the country was seeing "a bit of a better growth prospect" than other G7 nations.

Healey said: "Despite conflicts in the Middle East and Europe hitting people across the world, today's figures offer more proof of Britain's resilience in the face of these global shocks.

"This week the IMF have upgraded UK growth for 2026 and said that our fiscal discipline stands out with the lowest deficit in the G7 forecast by 2029."

He promised to build on the UK's debt reduction plans, which were praised by the IMF, and use the Budget to "provide some breathing space for today, and offer fresh hope for the future".

The Conservatives said the economic growth figures "conceal worrying trends in key sectors as we approach a crucial Budget".

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: "Construction has now shrunk for four months in a row, with private housebuilding falling fastest. Labour promised to get Britain building, but they are failing."

He called for Healey to cut taxes and reduce red tape.

Not building a third runway at Heathrow Airport would be a "huge missed opportunity" for the UK, the boss of the country's busiest airport has warned.

Thomas Woldbye told BBC Radio 4's Today programme it would be "good to know" the government's position on the project, after Prime Minister Andy Burnham refused to say whether he backed expansion.

The airport's chief executive said if its owners could not invest in a third runway, the money "will be invested somewhere else in the world", suggesting a decision would be made in the new year.

The Department for Transport said it was reviewing responses to a consultation and was "considering the appropriate next steps".

A spokesperson added that the government supported airport expansion "across the country where this can contribute to growth and opportunity, while meeting the tests on the environment".

They said expanding Heathrow had the "potential to deliver around £40 billion in economic benefits across the country".

Building a third runway at Heathrow has been debated for decades. The project has proved controversial, facing steep opposition from local residents, politicians and climate campaigners.

Last year, then-chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the government-backed expansion, saying that "a third runway is badly needed", and that the government could not "duck the decision any longer".

Heathrow Airport is owned by a consortium of investors, the largest of which is French private equity firm Ardian. Others include the Qatar Investment Authority, Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and the China Investment Corporation.

"If they cannot invest in Heathrow... then that money will be invested somewhere else in the world," Woldbye said.

"It's not about allocating this money elsewhere. It's private money. It's not public money. So hence, it will not go into the UK. I think that would be really a sad, huge missed opportunity for this country."

A third runway would mean demolishing hundreds of homes, diverting rivers, and rerouting the M25 motorway between junctions 14 and 15 through a tunnel under the new runway. It is estimated it would cost £33bn to build.

Heathrow serves more than 80 million travellers a year with its four passenger terminals and two runways. The number of flights, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average, if a third runway is built.

This additional traffic would potentially lead to a huge surge in revenue for the airport's owners, and Heathrow has argued the expansion would provide a "huge economic boost" and create jobs.

The new runway was scheduled to open by 2035, subject to plans being submitted and approved, but Heathrow has since suggested it would be delayed by four years to 2039 due to planning and regulatory issues.

Whether the new-look government still backs a third runway is not yet clear. Burnham, who as Mayor of Greater Manchester opposed the scheme, said he believed the matter was "for London and Londoners".

"I think we ought to hear the voice of people there first. It's not right for me to just jump straight in on the back of the consultation," he said, speaking to the BBC last month .

Woldbye said he hoped the prime minister would "will come along" with the project, pointing out it was backed by the unions.

He added that a third runway was "not just for Londoners". "Benefits will be felt all over the country because our supply chain reaches all the way from the north all the way to the south of the UK."

Downing Street declined to comment on Woldbye's remarks.

Questioned about the noise impact on nearby communities of more planes taking off and landing, Woldbye claimed Heathrow had seen a "stark" reduction in noise over the past 40 years and said the "trend will continue".

"My biggest concern is actually the years of uncertainty. And I think it's time that we give them certainty on what we want with this project so that we can move on and they can move on in their lives," he said.

Andy Burnham refuses to back third runway at Heathrow

Woldbye told the Today programme he had not yet met the current Chancellor John Healey, but if he did, he would outline that the airport "contributes dramatically to the economy" but that "we are now full".

"That means we will stop contributing or stop growing that contribution. If we want to avoid that, we need to now take this decision, move forward and continue the work of the previous government to move at speed and deliver this," he said.

The Department for Transport said it was still finalising its Airports National Policy Statement, which provides the basis for deciding whether to grant a new runway at Heathrow. It was last updated in 2018.

Woldbye said Heathrow was working on a planning application which has planned to submit in the next couple of years, but said any decision would be guided by government's the national policy statement.

A Saudi national who worked for OpenAI appeared in court this week for allegedly planting a secret recording device behind a TV in one of the tech giant's meeting rooms.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer, was arrested by the FBI and charged with using or attempting to use a device "to intercept oral communications".

As yet, it is not clear what he was planning to do with the recordings.

The engineer asked AI to help him listen in to discussions about AI, according to an official complaint (the document filed in court).

Between 17 August and 16 September, Alfozan had reportedly asked a productivity AI assistant several questions about meeting rooms and their availability.

Some detailed in the complaint include "how about external partners, where would they usually meet with OpenAI at" and "can you list today's meeting in this room".

The complaint also claimed that in September, Alfozan used a chatbot associated with his spouse to ask how to build and install a recording device and how to access it remotely.

Alfozan had worked at the firm for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant a recorder.

The room where the device was found was regularly used to hold meetings to discuss "highly confidential technical, commercial and strategic information" as well as OpenAI's "government engagements and commercial relationships", the complaint stated.

Alfozan had no authority to access or be involved with meetings in the room, the complaint states.

But CCTV footage recorded him near the conference room on eight separate occasions in September.

On 30 September, OpenAI staff discovered a "surreptitious audio recording device" behind a television - which had been wrapped in toilet paper.

A camera was placed in the conference room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering the room and appeared to look behind the television where the device had been inserted.

The complaint also stated that same day he allegedly left an unattended bag in a different room.

When security personnel opened it, it was found to contain "another recording device" similar to the one discovered, as well as Alfozan's wallet and ID.

In a post on X , external , OpenAI wrote it had used its own AI models to "understand the device and where it had come from".

It also said: "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data."

Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. The complaint said he was educated in the US and has been a legal permanent resident since 2020.

He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI has been terminated.

Alfozan's lawyer William Pernik told the BBC: "Like countless Americans, Mr Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream.

"These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible and any possible reasons why."

Pernik added: "In the meantime, we respectfully ask everyone to withhold judgment until full facts become known. Like every one of us, Mr Alfozan is presumed innocent, and what has been made public is an accusation, not a finding of guilt."

On Tuesday, Alfozan made his initial appearance in a federal court in California. A detention hearing is scheduled on 19 October to determine whether he should remain in custody while proceedings continue.

If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£190,000) fine.

Bank of America has been fined $1.2bn (£910m) for failing to detect potential money laundering and other illegal activity, the US Treasury Department said on Tuesday.

The banking giant failed to report over $5bn in suspicious activity to the government, $1bn of which posed national security and illicit finance risks, the Treasury said.

Those failures included not flagging transactions that possibly involved Chinese money laundering networks or trade-based laundering "with a substantial nexus to the southwest border", according to the Treasury.

"Our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators," Bank of America told the BBC.

The announcement came less 24 hours before Bank of America was due to announce its quarterly earnings on Wednesday morning.

"Our third-quarter results will include a non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2 billion impacting net income by approximately 17 cents per share," the bank said in an emailed statement.

"We have already dedicated substantial personnel and resources to our ongoing remediation efforts, and those costs are in the current expense base," it added.

In announcing the fine, the third-largest the department has ever imposed, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said: "When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks."

The Treasury said the bank overly relied on inquiries from outside parties like law enforcement and other financial institutions instead of its own internal controls.

This meant that it "effectively outsourced to third parties a substantial portion of its proactive detection and reporting obligations," the department said.

As part of the settlement, Bank of America admitted that it "willfully violated" the Bank Secrecy Act by failing to maintain a compliant anti-money laundering programme, conduct required due diligence on foreign correspondent accounts and file suspicious activity reports, the Treasury said.

The $1.2bn fine included penalties imposed by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC).

The OCC's $750m fine marked the biggest penalty it has ever levied.

OFAC said its settlement with the bank was tied to 475 apparent violations of sanctions programmes including those on Russia and Iran, narcotics, and global terrorism.

The settlement amount of $11.6m reflected the determination that Bank of America's apparent violations were "non-egregious", OFAC said.

Under-30s have described missing out on being able to "let loose and mess around" because of a "bleak" lack of nightlife where they live.

Henry Gannon said that growing up in Woking he had seen places for young people to gather and socialise "die away".

"Communal areas just seem to have vanished," he added.

Woking once had multiple late-night venues - now it does not have any traditional dedicated nightclubs left in the town centre.

Gannon blamed the situation on the cost of living crisis, which he said was "pricing out" those in their 20s from enjoying themselves.

"There isn't really anything to do for younger people who often don't have much expendable income," he said.

Alternative options, the 23-year-old added, were "Wetherspoons, sitting in the park or getting a prohibitively expensive taxi back from another town or city".

"I feel like I am missing out on a crucial part of being my age, which is being able to let loose, mess around and enjoy life.

A quarter of UK towns have lost all their nightclubs, the Night Time Industries Association (NTIA) said in 2025.

It added that one in six towns have no late-night venues left.

"These figures are a stark warning of the systematic erosion of Britain's nightlife infrastructure," said NTIA CEO Michael Kill.

"We are facing a national cultural crisis.

"The damage, as we see it, is increasingly irreversible. Once these venues disappear, they rarely return."

Adam said the nightlife situation in Tonbridge - where the last club closed several years ago - was "pretty minimal".

"There are some nice pubs and small bars, though most things close around midnight," he said.

But the 29-year-old, originally from the US, said he was drawn to Kent town as it was "quieter and more relaxed".

Still, Adam said, the lack of nightlife forced younger people to go elsewhere for a night out, which impacted the local economy.

"It is definitely a missed opportunity," he added.

While he recognised nightclubs were spaces for meeting others, Adam said there was also a trend of younger people going out and drinking less - which was good for their health.

The twenty-somethings going out - in the gym

The BBC previously heard from under-30s that were opting out of drinking culture and getting their "social fix" from the gym .

They said that alcohol-free socialising was empowering, avoided hangovers and let them meet like-minded people.

Others have also pointed to a cultural shift with more people skipping clubs for sober social events .

Finn Ashcroft, from Chichester in West Sussex, said after Covid "people were finding it harder to get out and socialise".

However, he said it was important to emphasise that many under-30s were "making do" without clubs and instead creating their own events.

While its traditional nightclubs had closed, Ashcroft said Chichester had plenty of spaces that could be used for music and dancing.

He told the BBC he had set up the event companies C-Side Sounds and Strictly Grooves to "push music locally" in these spaces.

"Students were champing at the bit for somewhere to go," he said.

"We've definitely helped nurture nightlife within the city."

The 22-year-old said the "most important thing" people looking for more nightlife where they live could do was "be vocal about it".

"They have the power to [get] local councils and governing bodies to make sure there are spaces for people... to make memories together."

About 400 postmen and women are leaving Royal Mail per week, according to the Communication Workers Union (CWU), who claims this number has gone up since the company introduced a new delivery system earlier this year.

The CWU says the firm had been losing about 330 postal staff a week from a workforce of 83,000 before it rolled out DM26, which reorganised routes to improve delivery performance.

The union claims the new system is not working in hundreds of offices, and BBC Your Voice has heard from staff warning of a "nightmare" Christmas ahead as the number of parcels increases.

Royal Mail says the reforms are part of its plan to deliver a more "efficient and financially sustainable" service.

Over the last year we've been in touch with more than 30 postal staff in all four nations of the UK, as they have switched over to DM26.

It allows for second class post to only be delivered every other weekday, and is supposed to guarantee first class mail and parcels are delivered every day, by putting workers into groups of three and changing the walking pattern of rounds.

But posties speaking to us anonymously say parcels are still being prioritised, letters left behind, and time wasted in sorting and dividing mail into first and second class.

"I didn't take any first class mail out on my last shift because I was on a road that's been behind for weeks," a worker in the West Midlands told me. "But I'm sure a manager would have ticked a box to say all first class mail went out."

A Royal Mail spokesperson said the company always worked to ensure all mail - both letters and parcels - were delivered on time.

Only three-quarters of first class mail delivered on time

Royal Mail letters sit undelivered 'for weeks' as parcels prioritised, staff say

Some postal workers we've spoken to say the new model is also increasing their workload.

We asked eight workers in different areas to track their average step counts. Since the switchover all their steps increased by a quarter or even a third, often up to around 25,000 steps a day.

Several fear this Christmas will be a "nightmare".

"We all think this Christmas will be the worst ever, for us and our customers," said one postman in the East Midlands.

Bryn Dymott delivered post in the village of Wootton in Bedfordshire for nine years. For the most part he loved the job. But he left the company in July saying he couldn't face another "shambolic" Christmas.

"People put things in the post for them to be delivered, not for them to be delayed because Royal Mail hasn't got the systems in place and enough people to get them delivered."

Bryn says he wanted to speak out after leaving the company because he was sick of the fact that posties aren't able to say what's really happening.

He says the company is "proving it's impossible to have four people's work done by three people. It shouldn't really come as a surprise."

So far DM26 has been introduced in about 1,000 of Royal Mail's 1,200 delivery offices.

Now the CWU has told its members to pause further roll-out of the new system until a plan can be agreed with Royal Mail to address problems.

The union says that while it is operating successfully in around 500 offices, it has run into significant problems in hundreds of others.

"Put simply, if a boat is already taking on water, adding more passengers is unlikely to solve the problem," says Martin Walsh of the CWU.

The union said most Royal Mail workers leaving the company were believed to be new starters on part-time contracts, but also said there had been an increase in staff on legacy contracts departing.

Royal Mail, on the other hand, says the new system is on track to be up and running in all offices by Christmas.

It says the roll-out is 90% complete and that it is now delivering to "95% of addresses every day across the UK, up from 88% before the roll-out. The roll-out continues across our network and we expect quality of service to improve as deployment progresses."

The company says it is hiring, as usual, an additional 22,000 temporary workers over the Christmas period.

Royal Mail has battled with increased competition and falling demand for letter deliveries in recent years, and last week announced plans to cut 2,500 head office and other supporting roles by the end of 2027.

The company has also faced years of criticism from politicians and the public over slow letter deliveries - something which has continued since the new system has been rolled out.

The regulator Ofcom has fined Royal Mail more than £37m in the last three years for missing delivery targets.

But some MPs think it is time for a new approach, and a group of them will meet the regulator later on Wednesday.

"We need to think outside the box," Dave Robertson, Labour MP for Lichfield, Burntwood and the Villages in Staffordshire.

"We need to bring as many people to the table on this to make sure we come up with a long-term solution because what's been tried up to now clearly isn't working."

An Ofcom spokesperson said not only has it issued fines to Royal Mail in recent years but it has also demanded an improvement plan and reformed the obligations imposed on the company, adding: "We will continue to hold it to account using the full extent of the powers available to us."

Postal Services Minister Kate Dearden said Royal Mail's improvement plan was "a step in the right direction, but it must deliver tangible improvements for customers. We will continue to hold them to account on their performance."

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has said she is "minded to intervene" in the proposed £1.6bn deal for Sky to buy ITV's media and entertainment division.

Nandy said there were reasonable grounds to believe the deal could affect free expression in the media and the variety of Britain's news landscape.

Sky said it would "carefully consider" a letter from the culture secretary and "engage constructively" with the review into the deal.

"We remain confident that bringing Sky and ITV's media and entertainment business together will create a stronger British media," it said.

ITV welcomed the letter and said the deal would help it "compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries".

The two companies announced in July that Sky had agreed to buy ITV's broadcasting business, including its free-to-air TV channels and the ITV X streaming service.

The deal does not include ITV's production arm, ITV Studios, which makes popular programmes such as Love Island and I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.

It would give Sky access to millions more viewers, while bosses hope it would help both compete with streaming giants such as Netflix.

What Sky buying ITV could mean for your favourite shows

But Nandy has told Sky and ITV that she is considering issuing a public interest intervention notice (PIIN) to the competition watchdog, forcing it to investigate the tie-up.

In a letter to both companies, she said she was minded to order the investigation so the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) could address public interest considerations including:

The need for free expression of opinion in news media

The need for a range of views in news media across the UK

The need for a range of people controlling the media across the UK

The need for a wide range of programmes to be offered across the UK

The letter said Nandy recognised Sky News and ITV News were two of the most prominent sources of television news in the UK, with a joint 26% share of viewers.

Consumers would still have access to other sources of news such as the BBC and Channel 4, it added.

But Nandy believes that, over time, the tie-up could undermine the range of views available to viewers, with 86% of the news market controlled by the BBC and Sky/ITV.

The North of England could be particularly hard hit as well as nations of the UK other than England and those from lower socio-economic backgrounds, the letter argued.

This is because their main source of news is broadcast news, it added.

Sky and ITV have been given until 20 October to respond to the culture secretary's concerns.

A Sky spokesperson said: "We have already made clear commitments to protect ITV's identity, its free-to-air services and public service broadcasting obligations, and to ensure ITV News and Sky News remain distinct editorial voices."

An ITV spokesperson said: "We welcome the publication of the secretary of state's 'minded to' issue a public interest intervention notice letter as was expected and look forward to fully co-operating in the process.

"This is another important milestone in the regulatory review process towards creating a UK player with the scale and resources to better compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries."

Nandy's intervention would be made under a new public interest consideration.

This would need legislation to be brought forward, given that current laws do not cover the effect of a merger on streaming or on-demand programmes.

She said: "If I decide to intervene on the basis of this new public interest consideration, I will bring forward legislation... to extend the application of the public interest consideration relating to the availability of a wide range of broadcasting to on-demand programmes."

The number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz has hit a record high, BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows.

Twelve vessels were attacked between 5 and 11 October - the largest number of weekly strikes reported to the UK's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency since the US-Israeli war with Iran began. The previous week saw 10 ships reporting attacks.

Six of the vessels were struck last Sunday, according to the UKMTO - a one-day high. So far this week, there have been four reported attacks.

As the number of strikes has risen, the recovery in oil shipments through the strait seen last month has slowed, industry data suggests.

BBC Verify collated incident reports published by the UKMTO on its website and created a timeline based on the first date cited in each report. This is approximate because some incidents use the date of the attack and some the date on which it was reported.

Experts say Tehran has been attacking ships in an effort to assert greater control over the waterway as the US military has increased the number of tankers it is shepherding through the south of the strait to evade Iranian strikes.

Iran is also carrying out more attacks on vessels further away from the Strait of Hormuz, according to experts.

The US military's Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, posted on social media that despite the attacks "commercial traffic continues to flow through the Strait of Hormuz with co-ordinated protection from US forces and regional partners".

The aftermath of one of Sunday's six reported attacks was captured in verified footage showing the Nicaragua-flagged tanker Petro Dolphin on fire, as filmed by the crew on a smaller boat nearby.

The vessel was struck by a drone close to the Sohar Anchorage, Oman, more than 250km (150 miles) from the strait, according to the maritime intelligence firm Vanguard.

Eleven Indian seafarers were rescued but two are still missing, the Forward Seamen's Union of India said.

Attacks have continued this week with the container ship GFS Pride sinking after a strike by an unknown projectile in the strait on Tuesday. Twenty-one crew were safely evacuated.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) published footage of what appeared to be the same ship sinking. It said the vessel was carrying "2,500 containers of contraband" and had taken an "unauthorised route".

Middle East oil exports have slowed as the number of ship strikes has risen.

About 12.6 million barrels per day went through the strait on 13 October, below the 15 million reported at the end of September, data from trade intelligence firm Kpler shows. This compares with a pre-war baseline of some 17 million barrels per day.

The recent increase in attacks comes as US Navy data indicates the number of vessels given assistance to navigate the Strait of Hormuz during the first 10 days of October was up 85% compared with the same period in August.

Most of the oil being shipped from Gulf Arab states recently has been carried using a "shuttle" system where a fleet of tankers load up and sail through the strait before transferring their cargo to larger tankers in the Gulf of Oman.

These shuttle ships use a route close to Oman's coastline. Iran says this is "unauthorised" and insist vessels take an alternative route closer to its own shore.

So-called assisted transits were a key factor in helping drive oil flows from the Middle East back towards pre-war levels in September. This does not include Iranian exports which have completely stalled as a result of the US blockade of Iranian ports and ships.

Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, said Iran has "evolved its strategy" in response to this loosening of its control over the strait and has been carrying out "near daily or multiple attacks every single day".

"The aim here is to stop the ships going through and to deter others," he added.

The IRGC's navy has said strikes would not be "limited to the Strait of Hormuz" and later announced a "new deployment formation" across the region, according to state media.

Martin Kelly told BBC Verify that Iran is widening its attacks and targeting ships near the coast of Gulf Arab states and in the Gulf of Oman.

A tanker was struck by multiple projectiles north of Qatar on Thursday 8 October, more than 500km (310 miles) from the strait, resulting in multiple reported casualties, according to Vanguard.

Another tanker was attacked close to the UAE town of Al-Jazirah al-Hamra on Friday 9 October, Vanguard said.

Verified footage shows crew members running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rises over the ship.

Steve Cargil's family has farmed the flat, dry land around Uvalde, a small city in southwest Texas, since 1953.

Cargil, 67, had always assumed that one of his three children would eventually take it over, the way he had from his father.

But that assumption took a hit one night in 2018 after a violent hailstorm.

Cargil and his son, Ryan, had spent months nursing crops of cabbage and onions to harvest. Then a storm rolled through and destroyed them overnight.

"I remember my son saying, 'Dad, I just don't know if I can do this. You do everything right, and we work so hard, and you come out one morning and it's all gone'," Cargil says.

Cargil's farm was at risk of ending with him, he says, with none of his three children wanting to farm full time. For years, that left him wondering what would happen to the land, and to his own retirement, since farmers rarely have a pension to fall back on.

Then in 2001 Cargil signed a deal to lease 600 acres of his land, about a quarter of the total, to a company called OCI Energy which built a vast solar farm.

"Never in my wildest dreams did I think that a solar project would be on my farm," Cargil says. Looking back now, he calls it a blessing.

The lease, which pays Cargil $200,000 (£150,000) a year, has let him keep his farm running through a punishing drought. He has been able to concentrate his water irrigation allowance on the land he still farms, and he has stopped losing sleep over rises in the price of things such as diesel and fertiliser. "It's changed my life."

Texas, which remains the largest oil producer in the US, earlier this year overtook California to become the country's biggest generator of electricity from solar farms. , external

And in March of last year, more electricity was produced by solar in Texas than from coal for the first time, according to the US Energy Information Administration.

On hot afternoons, when demand for power peaks, solar is now regularly supplying around a third of the electricity used across Texas, says Mark Stover, executive director of the Texas Solar and Storage Association.

He says that the solar boom is being driven by two main things. Firstly, it is cheap and quick to connect solar farms to Texas' power grid, which is separate to the rest of the US. Secondly, Texas has a huge and growing appetite for electricity, driven by a burgeoning population.

Between 2015 and 2025, Texas's population increased by 15.8%, , external making it one of the fastest-growing states in the nation.

"We need a whole lot of power in Texas, and we need it quickly," Stover says.

Solar has also become inexpensive. James Scott, vice president of project development at OCI, says the technology has had years of small manufacturing gains that brought the price down to the point where it is now the cheapest way to generate power in the state.

"No one would have believed that 20 years ago," Scott says.

Once a project is built, he says, the price of the electricity it produces can be fixed for decades, since the fuel, sunlight, is free.

"We'll charge you $40 a megawatt hour for the next 25 years," Scott says, adding that large buyers such as Amazon and Apple value being able to lock in a price for that long.

By contrast, new coal plants in the US produce power at nearly $90 megawatts per hour, says the Energy Information Administration.

Farmers have become central to that growth because solar developers need large stretches of flat land.

Stover says the industry is now paying out multigenerational income to families through leases that typically run 25 to 30 years and rise in value each year, letting some retire, set up family trusts, or simply keep a farm solvent.

Stover argues solar's footprint is smaller than critics assume. "The industry is utilizing less than 0.15% of Texas land," he says.

Yet solar has its opponents. In Franklin County, in northeast Texas, a small group of residents has spent the past few years fighting its growth.

BF Hicks, a local lawyer whose family has owned land in the county since the 1800s, says he watched neighbours sign 30-year leases with solar companies and bulldozers clear centuries-old oak trees near his property.

He describes a summer when smoke from burning cleared land hung over his town for weeks. "It got real personal," he says, when a solar farm was built next to his family's cemetery. His relatives have been buried here dating back two centuries.

David Truesdale, a retired federal law enforcement agent who moved to the county to get away from city life, says he became involved after learning that a neighbouring solar project would sit near his home. And that under Texan law no environmental review was required.

"We're destroying the world as we're trying to save it," Truesdale says of the land clearing he has seen. He also points to the large lithium-ion battery units installed alongside many solar farms, drawing a comparison to fires that have occasionally engulfed similar batteries in electric bikes.

"If one of those things catches fire, they go off in series, so each one will progressively cause another one to go off," he says.

Both men say their objections are not about politics. Franklin County is solidly conservative, but its residents helped push through one of the state's first county-level moratoriums on new solar construction, before it was later rescinded under legal pressure from developers.

Their complaints echo a broader unease that has followed solar's expansion into rural Texas - worries about visual impact, water runoff after land is cleared, and battery storage units that scorch their land.

President Trump has called solar and wind power "farmer destroying" and moved to unwind tax credits for renewable projects.…

A Jersey politician said she thought cost-of-living pressures were not considered by the government when it chose to end a trial of free fruit in primary schools.

Since 2024 children in four primary schools have been able to get apples, bananas and other fruit as part of the pilot scheme.

Deputy Louise Doublet said: "To have that taken away at a time when the cost of living is still increasing I think has been quite hard for some families".

The education minister ended the trial because not enough children were eating the fruit and it was leading to a lot of wastage. The Government of Jersey has been approached for a comment.

The government announced in September fresh fruit would be included in a school food programme that provides hot school meals for government primary schools.

Minister for Education and Lifelong Learning Catherine Curtis previously said the free fruit scheme was leading to "a lot of wastage" and parents "actually asked" for fruit to be incorporated into the school food programme instead.

The topic was debated 29 September , external in the States Assembly.

Doublet said the minister had responded to her questions in the assembly "centred around the evidence and she informed the assembly that it hadn't resulted in much of an increase in children actually consuming fruit and vegetables and I do accept that".

But she added she did not think benefits in terms of cost of living were measured by the scheme.

"Personally I would like to see more investment in healthy food especially if it's locally grown food to help families with the cost of living," she said.

When asked about the contract with UK company Apetito Limited to provide hot school meals for government primary schools across Jersey she said it was the "best available option".

She added she understood people's concerns around the freshness of the food but her "understanding is that the meals are actually frozen rather than artificially preserved".

"I would like to see these funded meals extended further because it hits the cost of living for parents and... provides healthy meals for children," she said.

A civil servant is accused of earning almost £350,000 by juggling five full-time public sector roles - using sick notes and working from home to cope with the workload.

Kashim Chowdhury allegedly held multiple government jobs between February 2020 and September 2023, earning £350,000 overall.

The jury at Southwark Crown Court has been told he wore white make-up during a video call with his boss to try to look ill, but the make-up began peeling off his skin.

Chowdury, a 55-year-old from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud, which he denies. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain.

The jury was told that Chowdhury got jobs by making ''false representations'' about his employment status whilst applying. Over three years he held overlapping jobs at Tower Hamlets Council in east London, the Home Office, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the UK Health Security Agency and the Department of Health and Social Care.

The jury was told that in 2023 his manager at the Health Security Agency, Aleesha Adams, organised a video call with him to discuss his sick leave.

Ms Adams claims Chowdhury was wearing make-up on his face to appear ill - and that during the meeting the make-up started to separate on his forehead showing his real skin underneath. At the time of the call he is alleged to have been paid for five full time jobs.

Lucy Organ, for the prosecution, told the court: "There could be no doubt about it, the defendant had applied make-up to his face for this Teams meeting to try and pretend to his line manager that he was unwell.

"This almost laughable incident demonstrates, we say, quite how far the defendant was willing to go in his deceit."

Prosecutors say Chowdhury "exploited" the work from home culture that began during the Covid pandemic. The court was told that Chowdhury had told his employers that he had to work from home to care for his "unwell" mother.

But the prosecutor, Ms Organ, said his workload eventually became "too much to cope with" and his performance suffered.

The court heard that he was signed off work from some jobs due to "mixed anxiety and a depressive disorder", but he did not hand his sick note to all his employers.

Jurors heard that the alleged fraud came to light after the National Fraud Initiative alerted Defra to them.

Wayfair is among three firms which have been fined £6m in total by the competition watchdog for illegally using misleading sales tactics – with some customers set to receive refunds.

The online furniture retailer was fined £4.8m for misleading customers with time-limited offers, while online electronics seller Appliances Direct was fined £1.2m for the same practice, the Competition Markets Authority (CMA) said.

Meanwhile, Gold's Gym has been fined £48,000 for not telling customers the total price of its memberships.

It and Appliances Direct have been ordered to refund customers a total of £440,000. Wayfair and Appliances Direct said the CMA's fines were disproportionate.

Gold's Gym has been contacted for comment.

Thousands of Appliances Direct customers will receive refunds of £25 each on average while 726 Gold's Gym customers will get refunds of up to £50, according to the CMA.

The watchdog said customers do not need to take any action and both companies will contact those affected customers about refunds.

Appliances Direct has been told to pay refunds by 11 March, while Gold's Gym has been given a deadline of 29 March.

The CMA said Wayfair, Appliances Direct, and Gold's Gym had "engaged constructively" with its investigation. They all admitted to breaking the law and agreed to settle the case early, it added.

The watchdog said their co-operation reduced the firms' fines by 40%.

The CMA's fines are the result of an investigation it launched last November into online pricing .

Eight firms under investigation over online pricing

AA and BSM ordered to refund learner drivers for hidden fees

A Wayfair spokeswoman said the penalty was "excessive" but that "we take the CMA's findings seriously and we chose to settle so we can continue to focus on serving our customers".

Nick Glynne, chief executive of Buy it Direct, which owns Appliances Direct and several other online retailers, accepted that its practices were wrong, but said the firm should have simply been given "a rap on the knuckles" instead.

Glynne said the CMA's process for calculating the fine was a "black box" and that it only settled because appealing was too expensive, accusing the watchdog of pressure tactics.

"When one body is investigator, prosecutor, judge and jury, it needs an exceptional commitment to fairness, restraint and proportionality. That is not what we experienced," he added.

Hayley Fletcher, senior director for consumer protection at the CMA, said: "At a time when many households are carefully managing their budgets, people shouldn't lose out because of misleading sales tactics.

"Businesses must treat their customers fairly and make sure they comply with the law - or risk hefty fines."

The CMA's investigation found that the three companies had misled customers in different ways.

Wayfair had advertised products as if they would disappear the next day, through phrases like "Here Today, Gone Tomorrow" and countdown timers.

However, the CMA said many products remained available at the same price or lower after the stated deadline, meaning the time-limited offer was false.

Meanwhile, the regulator said Appliances Direct had automatically opted customers into services such as recycling old machines.

Gold's Gym was fined for failing to include joining fees in the total price of gym memberships or not making its total price clear to customers, the CMA said.

Artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic saw its revenue surge by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.7bn) in the three months to the end of September, the BBC understands.

The figures were reportedly revealed by the Claude-developer as it briefed prospective investors on Wednesday at its headquarters in San Francisco as it lays the groundwork for a stock market listing, which is expected to take place before the end of the year.

It comes as some tech stocks, including firms that make the chips and other hardware that power data centres, have come under pressure over concerns about the large amounts of money being spent on AI infrastructure.

An Anthropic spokesperson declined to comment.

Anthropic's revenue has risen in successive quarters this year, from $4.7bn in the first three months to $11.6bn the following period.

The company also reportedly said that it made a profit for the second quarter in a row.

Its revenue figures, along with those of rival OpenAI, offer an important gauge of the AI industry's growth and ability to finance the infrastructure needed to develop the technology.

Stocks in some US technology companies fell on Wednesday over concerns around investments in AI.

Share in chip makers - including AMD, Nvidia and Intel - fell sharply.

In Asia, shares in Japanese tech investment firm Softbank fell by 9% on Thursday morning. South Korean semiconductor giants were also down, with Samsung falling by 8.4% and SK Hynix dropping by more than 6%.

South Korea's tech-heavy Kospi index was 7.6% lower in morning trading.

The falls come after remarks by Hock Tan, the chief executive of US tech manufacturer Broadcom, over AI spending.
